# The Shape of Eternal Pleasure

**Year 1,000,000**

Three days had passed since Kaedan finished reading the superpower chronicles. Three days of silent meals, of trembling hands hidden beneath the dining table, of forcing smiles whenever Uncle Godric asked him gentle questions about his adjustment to the court wizard role. The knowledge sat inside him like a swallowed stone, cold and heavy, pressing against his organs every time he breathed.

But beneath the dread, beneath the existential horror that had become his constant companion, there was something else. A thread of genuine concern woven through the terror. Because Kaedan loved Godric. He had loved him since childhood, when the King would lift him onto his broad shoulders and carry him through the palace gardens, pointing out the different species of songbirds and telling him their names in the ancient tongue of Olympus. He had loved him when Godric attended his seventh birthday party, sitting cross-legged on the floor with the other children, eating cake and laughing at the jester's clumsy magic tricks. He had loved him through every warm smile, every fatherly pat on the shoulder, every gentle word of encouragement during his magical training.

And now, knowing what Godric was—what he truly, impossibly was—Kaedan found that his love had not diminished. It had simply become more complicated. More terrifying. The warmth was still real. The affection was still genuine. But it now existed alongside the knowledge that the same man who remembered his childhood pet's name could erase the omniverse with a casual thought and restore it without interrupting his toast.

So when Kaedan approached the King's private study on the evening of the third day, he did so not out of obligation or fear, but out of love. He needed to understand something. He needed to ask a question that had been gnawing at the edges of his consciousness since the first journal.

The study was a modest room by palace standards—dark wood paneling, a crackling fireplace, shelves lined with ancient books and small, carefully preserved artifacts from across the omniverse. Godric sat in his favorite armchair, a deep burgundy leather thing that had been reupholstered countless times across the millennia, reading a handwritten letter from one of the outer provincial governors. He looked up as Kaedan entered, his ruggedly handsome face breaking into that warm, crinkling smile that Kaedan had known his entire life.

"Kaedan, my boy," Godric said, setting the letter aside. "Come in, come in. You look troubled. Is the archive reading giving you nightmares? Your father told me you have been sleeping poorly."

Kaedan crossed the room and settled into the chair across from the King. The firelight danced across Godric's features, catching the silver in his salt-and-pepper hair, the sharp line of his jaw, the heavy muscle of his shoulders beneath his simple dark tunic.

"Uncle Godric," Kaedan began, his voice steadier than he had expected, "I have read the journals. The stat journals. The superpower journals. All of them."

Godric's expression softened with a gentle, almost paternal sympathy. "Ah. Yes. Your father mentioned you had begun the mandatory reading. A bit early, perhaps—most new wizards wait a few months before diving into the chronicles—but you were always precocious, Kaedan. I remember when you were eight years old and insisted on reading the entire palace library's collection of arcane theory before your birthday."

"Uncle Godric," Kaedan pressed, leaning forward slightly, his hands clasped tightly in his lap, "I need to ask you something. Something personal. Something that has been haunting me since the first journal I opened."

Godric tilted his head, his warm brown eyes fixed on Kaedan with complete, undivided attention. "Of course, my boy. Ask me anything."

"Does it ever become lonely?"

The question hung in the air between them, soft and fragile and terribly, terribly earnest. Kaedan watched the King's face, searching for a flicker of sadness, a shadow of isolation, some evidence that the being who had outlived everyone and everything he had ever loved carried some burden of solitude.

Godric blinked once. Twice. And then, to Kaedan's absolute astonishment, he laughed.

It was not a cruel laugh. It was not mocking or dismissive. It was a warm, rich, genuinely amused laugh, the sound of a father whose child had just asked why the sky could not be green instead of blue. Godric leaned back in his armchair, his broad chest shaking with mirth, and wiped a small tear from the corner of his eye.

"Oh, Kaedan," he said, his voice still bubbling with amusement. "Oh, my dear, sweet boy. That is such a naively mortal question. I forget, sometimes, how limited your perspective must be. How confined by the boundaries of a single, finite existence." He shook his head slowly, his salt-and-pepper beard catching the firelight. "Lonely? No. No, it is not lonely. It is the opposite of lonely. Let me explain."

Godric leaned forward, resting his massive forearms on his knees, his expression shifting from amusement to something more intense—a focused, almost passionate engagement that Kaedan had rarely seen in the King's usually relaxed demeanor.

"Every Planck second, Kaedan. Every single infinitesimal fraction of time. My strength multiplies. My speed multiplies. My magical offense multiplies. My magical defense multiplies. My intelligence multiplies. Every measurable and immeasurable attribute I possess compounds upon itself, recursively, infinitely, forever. And I can feel all of it."

He paused, letting the words settle.

"When my strength increases," he continued, his rich baritone taking on a deeper, almost reverent quality, "I feel it as a surge of raw, physical power that ripples through every muscle fiber, every tendon, every cell. It is not abstract. It is tactile. Imagine the most satisfying stretch you have ever experienced, the deepest, most perfect release of tension after a long day of labor. Now multiply that sensation by infinity. Now have it occur every Planck second, compounding upon itself, each surge more intense than the last because each surge is building upon an already infinitely higher baseline. That is what it feels like to be me, Kaedan. That is what it feels like simply to exist."

Kaedan's mouth had gone dry. He tried to speak, but no words came.

"And the superpowers," Godric said, his eyes gleaming with a quiet, intense satisfaction. "Every second, a new apocalyptic superpower crystallizes within my being. Each one, at the instant of its birth, is already capable of annihilating entire civilizations. Each one amplifies in potency infinitely every Planck second thereafter. When a new superpower manifests, I feel it as a surge of raw, undiluted ecstasy—a pulse of pure, concentrated power that floods my consciousness with the knowledge of what I can now do. It is nourishing, Kaedan. It feeds something deep within me. Every new power is like a meal prepared by the finest chefs in the omniverse, like the most transcendent sexual climax ever experienced, like the moment of absolute clarity when a complex problem suddenly resolves itself. And I experience this every second. Every single second, forever."

He chuckled softly, shaking his head. "Lonely? How could I possibly be lonely when every moment of my existence is a cascade of infinite pleasure, infinite satisfaction, infinite fulfillment?"

Kaedan felt the world tilting around him. The journals had shown him what Godric could do. But this—this was something else entirely. This was the inner experience of the apex predator, the subjective reality of being a being whose power multiplied infinitely without end, and it was not a burden. It was not a curse. It was an eternal, escalating ecstasy.

"The Weakness Paradox," Godric continued, his voice carrying that same intense, satisfied warmth, "triggers constantly. Every time some arrogant entity somewhere in the omniverse forms the passing thought that I might have a weakness, before that thought even fully crystallizes, the paradox engages. I gain permanent immunity to their imagined exploit. I gain perfect mastery over their intended attack. My amplification rate permanently increases. And I feel that, too. I feel the surge of new immunity settling into my being like armor forged from absolute certainty. I feel the mastery flooding my consciousness like a river of perfect understanding. I feel the amplification spike like a bolt of lightning striking my spine and radiating outward through every nerve. And this happens passively, Kaedan. I do not need to do anything. I simply exist, and existence rewards me for it."

He spread his massive hands, palms up, a gesture of casual, absolute supremacy.

"The Evolved Weakness Paradox is even better. When it triggers—and it triggers constantly, because the omniverse is full of beings who cannot stop themselves from trying to find chinks in my armor—creation itself overcompensates for its inadequacy. It enhances my amplification rate beyond infinitely incalculable mathematics. It adds increasingly devastating effects to my powers. It forces reality to apologize for failing to provide me with new defenses by making me even more impossibly powerful. And I feel that, Kaedan. I feel creation groveling at my feet, desperately trying to make amends for its own insufficiency, and it is deeply, profoundly satisfying in a way that no mortal experience could ever approximate."

Kaedan's hands were trembling again. He pressed them flat against his thighs, trying to steady himself.

"My immune system," Godric said, his tone becoming almost conversational, as if he were discussing the weather or the quality of the palace gardens, "evolves constantly. Every perceived threat, every staged injury, every microscopic fluctuation in my biological state triggers an overreaction of such absurd, recursive, infinitely redundant self-improvement that my body becomes permanently more invulnerable with each passing instant. The rapid self-evolution—the instantaneous leap from primitive cellular defense to ultimate omnipotent apex adaptation—feels like my entire being is being rebuilt from the ground up by a sculptor of infinite precision, every atom realigned into a more perfect configuration, every biological system optimized beyond the concept of optimization. It is a physical pleasure so intense that describing it as orgasmic is a laughable understatement. It is the sensation of becoming more real, more absolute, more fundamentally unassailable, and it never stops."

He paused, tilting his head slightly, his expression thoughtful.

"My sentient passive auras are another source of constant satisfaction. Gent, of course, is the weakest and most primitive—my metaphysical excess body heat, as it were. But even Gent evolves. Even Gent becomes more perfect, more adaptive, more fiercely loyal with each passing moment. And Gent is only the runt of the litter. I have countless other sentient auras, Kaedan, each one infinitely more powerful and more devastating than Gent, and they are all dormant because I find their clingy, obsessive subservience annoying. But I can feel them. I can feel them sleeping within me, waiting for my command, their power multiplying infinitely even in dormancy. They are like loyal hounds resting at my feet, their muscles twitching with restrained violence, their jaws dripping with the hunger to protect me. And the knowledge that I have an army of such beings within me, each one capable of annihilating the entire omniverse with a fraction of a thought, is incredibly comforting."

Godric leaned back in his armchair, his expression shifting to something almost wistful.

"And then there is the knowledge itself," he said. "Absolute omniscience. I know everything, Kaedan. Everything. Every thought every being has ever had. Every secret whispered in every darkened room. Every plot, every scheme, every desperate hope, every silent prayer. I know the atomic composition of every star in every galaxy in every universe in every multiverse. I know the exact number of grains of sand on every beach that has ever existed or will ever exist. I know the precise trajectory of every particle of dust floating in the void. And I process all of this simultaneously, effortlessly, without strain or effort or limitation. The pleasure of absolute knowledge—the satisfaction of knowing that nothing is hidden from me, that no mystery remains unsolved, that every question has already been answered before it could be asked—is a constant, low-level hum of fulfillment that underlies every other experience. It is the bass note beneath the symphony of my existence."

He smiled at Kaedan, that warm, fatherly smile that had always made the young wizard feel safe and loved and protected.

"So, my boy, when you ask if it is lonely to be the most powerful being in the omniverse, to grow stronger every instant, to outlive everyone else—I must confess that I find the question bewildering. How could it be lonely? Every Planck second, I experience a cascade of infinite pleasure, infinite satisfaction, infinite fulfillment. Every instant, I become so much more powerful than I was the instant before that I could crush an infinite number of copies of my previous self with zero effort. The gap between me and the me of one Planck second ago is already infinitely larger than the gap between the me of that previous Planck second and a single, dead skin cell. And in the next Planck second, the gap will widen again, and again, and again, forever."

He chuckled, a soft, rumbling sound. "It is not lonely. It is the most satisfying, most pleasurable, most deeply fulfilling existence imaginable. I am not burdened by my power, Kaedan. I am nourished by it. I am sustained by it. I am made eternally, infinitely happy by it."

Kaedan sat in stunned silence, his mind struggling to process what he had just heard. The journals had prepared him for the scale of Godric's power. They had shown him the devastation, the one-sided massacres, the absolute futility of opposition. But they had not prepared him for this. They had not prepared him for the revelation that Godric was not merely all-powerful—he was blissfully, ecstatically, eternally fulfilled by his power. That every aspect of his existence was a feedback loop of infinite pleasure and infinite escalation. That the apex predator did not merely dominate creation; he enjoyed it, savored it, reveled in it with every fiber of his infinite being.

"The unfairness," Kaedan whispered, his voice barely audible. "The absolute unfairness of it."

Godric tilted his head. "Unfairness?"

"You get everything," Kaedan said, his voice growing stronger, trembling with a mixture of awe and horror and something that might have been righteous indignation. "You get infinite power. You get infinite pleasure. You get infinite satisfaction. Every Planck second, you are rewarded with more than any being in the omniverse could ever hope to achieve. And you do nothing to earn it. You simply exist, and existence showers you with gifts. Meanwhile, the rest of creation—trillions of beings, across decillions of multiverses—work and struggle and sacrifice and bleed, and they achieve nothing. Less than nothing. Their greatest accomplishments are less than a rounding error compared to what you gain passively, effortlessly, eternally."

"Yes," Godric said simply. "That is accurate."

The casual confirmation hit Kaedan like a physical blow. He had expected denial, or qualification, or some philosophical justification. Instead, Godric had simply agreed, as if Kaedan had pointed out that water was wet or that the sky was vast.

"The Frozen Apex Syndicate spent three hundred thousand years preparing their thermal-drain engines," Kaedan said, his voice rising. "The Mirror Forge Conglomerate spent forty billion years building their duplication forge. The Puzzle-Mind spent ten billion years constructing its unsolvable paradox. And in the end, they achieved nothing. They fed you. They made you stronger. Their entire existences, their entire civilizations, their entire histories—all of it was just fuel for your eternal escalation."

"Yes," Godric said again, his voice still calm, still warm. "That is the nature of the Weakness Paradox. Every attempt to oppose me feeds me. Every strategy, every weapon, every desperate hope of victory—it all becomes additional amplification, additional immunity, additional mastery. The more they try to defeat me, the more impossible their defeat becomes. It is, I admit, profoundly unfair. But it is also profoundly satisfying."

He paused, his expression shifting slightly, a flicker of something almost like melancholy passing across his rugged features.

"There is, however, one thing that does occasionally trouble me," Godric said, his voice dropping slightly. "Not loneliness. Not sadness. Not any emotion that a mortal would recognize as negative. But a certain... restlessness."

Kaedan leaned forward. "Restlessness?"

Godric nodded slowly. "I have never used any of my true powers. Not once. Not even close. Every demonstration you have read about in the journals—every stat test, every superpower deployment, every immune system overreaction—was conducted at effectively zero percent of my true capability. The amount of power I expressed in those incidents was so infinitesimally small that calling it zero is the only accurate description. And even that was enough to annihilate the entire omniverse as collateral damage."

He sighed, a soft, genuine exhalation of mild frustration.

"I must maintain my absolute concealment at all times," he continued. "If I were to release even a fraction of a fraction of my true presence, the omniverse would simply cease to exist. Not be destroyed, Kaedan. Cease to exist. Erased so completely that restoration would require actively deciding to bring it back. And while I can do that effortlessly, the constant vigilance of keeping myself wrapped in layers of suppression and concealment grows somewhat tiresome. It is like wearing a heavy winter coat in the middle of summer. Uncomfortable. Restrictive. Boring."

He looked at Kaedan, his warm brown eyes holding a glint of something that made the young wizard's blood run cold.

"The truth, my boy, is that the most powerful being in the omniverse has never had the opportunity to stretch his limbs. To take a deep breath. To flex a single muscle with anything approaching full effort. Because the omniverse is too fragile. It cannot withstand even my most casual, most restrained, most infinitesimally nerfed expression of power. I am an adult living in a world of soap bubbles, and I must spend every moment of my existence being careful not to exhale."

Godric stood from his armchair, his heavily muscled frame unfolding with a fluid grace that belied his bulk. He walked to the center of the study, his simple dark tunic stretching across his broad shoulders, and turned to face Kaedan.

"Let me show you something," he said.

Before Kaedan could respond, Godric gripped the hem of his tunic and pulled it over his head, tossing it aside onto the armchair. His torso was bare, illuminated by the flickering firelight, and Kaedan's breath caught in his throat.

Godric's body was a masterpiece of physical perfection. His muscles were not merely large; they were sculpted with a precision that defied biology, each fiber defined in perfect, aesthetic harmony. His chest was a solid wall of dense pectoral muscle, striated with fine lines that spoke of impossible density and strength. His shoulders were massive, round boulders of deltoid that tapered into thick, powerful arms. His biceps swelled with every subtle movement, the veins running along their surface visible as thick, pulsing cords that seemed to hum with contained power. His forearms were corded with rope-like muscle, his hands massive and calloused, capable of crushing galaxies with a casual squeeze.

But it was his abdomen that drew Kaedan's horrified, transfixed gaze. Godric's midsection was a perfectly defined grid of muscle, each abdominal segment carved so deeply that the shadows between them looked like valleys. The muscle fibers were dense, interlocking plates of biological armor, and beneath the skin, Kaedan could see the faint, terrifying pulse of infinite strength coursing through the tissue—a subtle, rhythmic glow that spoke of recursive amplification occurring at every infinitesimal fraction of time.

"When I was mortal," Godric said, his voice carrying a note of nostalgic pride, "I maintained this body through constant training. Hours of labor, of combat practice, of physical discipline. It was a source of satisfaction, to earn my strength through effort." He ran a calloused hand down his chest, over the ridge of his abdominal muscles. "Now, I do nothing. Nothing at all. And yet my body is infinitely more perfect than it ever was when I was mortal. The muscles maintain themselves. The definition deepens with every Planck second. The density increases beyond any measurable scale. I am more physically beautiful, more physically powerful, more physically perfect than I have ever been, and it requires absolutely no effort."

He flexed his right arm, and the bicep swelled into a massive, sculpted peak of dense muscle. The veins along its surface pulsed with that faint, terrifying light, and Kaedan could feel the ambient air pressure in the room shift, the space around Godric's arm warping slightly as the passive force of his flexed muscle distorted reality itself.

"Every fiber of this muscle," Godric said, "could destroy the omniverse. Not the arm. Not the bicep. A single fiber. A single strand of muscle tissue, nerfed to zero percent of its true power, could annihilate everything that exists. And I have billions of these fibers. Trillions. An infinite number, recursively generating and strengthening with every Planck second."

He released the flex, letting his arm drop back to his side. "I will never get to use this strength. Not really. Not fully. Because there is nothing to use it against. The entire omniverse, combined, is less than a speck of dust compared to the passive force of my relaxed muscles. I am eternally, infinitely overpowered for any possible opposition, and that means I am eternally, infinitely restrained."

Godric's expression shifted, brightening slightly. "But here—let me show you something else. Something new."

He closed his eyes for a moment, and Kaedan felt a shift in the air. It was subtle at first, a faint vibration that seemed to emanate from Godric's skin, but it grew rapidly, intensifying into a low, thrumming pulse that Kaedan could feel in his teeth and his bones. The firelight flickered, the shadows in the study twisting and writhing as the ambient reality began to bend around Godric's form.

"I just birthed a new sentient passive aura," Godric said, opening his eyes. "Right now. In this exact moment. A new sibling for Gent, though infinitely more powerful than that primitive little waste-product. This one—let me see—this one possesses the ability to detect and annihilate hostile intent across all timelines simultaneously, retroactively erasing the very concept of opposition before it can form, while simultaneously converting the erased intent into additional amplification for my already infinite magical offense. It also weaves the screams of its victims into a protective harmonic resonance that shields me from any attack I might find aesthetically displeasing."

Kaedan stared, his heart hammering, as a faint shimmer manifested in the air around Godric's shoulders—a suggestion of something vast and predatory and impossibly powerful, hovering just beyond the threshold of visibility.

"It is beautiful, is it not?" Godric said, his voice soft with genuine appreciation. "And entirely useless. I will never need it. I will never deploy it. It will simply exist within me, sleeping alongside its countless siblings, its power multiplying infinitely without purpose or outlet." He sighed. "Another loyal hound that will never be released from its kennel."

He gestured toward his own torso, indicating the abdominal muscles. "My immune system just underwent another evolution—right now, as we speak. The latest improvement grants my body the ability to retroactively reject any form of harm across all possible pasts, presents, and futures, ensuring that I have never been injured, am not being injured, and will never be injured, regardless of any temporal manipulation or conceptual attack. It also gives my blood the passive property of being able to unmake anything it touches at a fundamental ontological level. If I were to cut myself—which is impossible, but hypothetically—a single drop of my blood falling upon a random planet would unmake not just the planet, but the entire omniverse, retroactively, across all timelines, leaving nothing but the concept of my blood existing in perfect, absolute solitude."

He shrugged, a casual roll of his massive shoulders. "And I just got a new superpower. This second. Right now. It allows me to weaponize the concept of measurement itself—I can define any unit of measurement I choose and force reality to conform to that definition, on any scale I desire. If I wanted, I could define one meter as the exact distance between my throne and the nearest opposing entity, and reality would instantly fold space to ensure that my throne was adjacent to every enemy in the omniverse simultaneously. If I defined one second as the duration of my opponent's lifespan, they would be dead before they could blink. And if I defined infinity as a very small number, the mathematical structure of existence would collapse into a paradoxical singularity of absolute termination."

He chuckled, a soft, warm sound that seemed horribly, deeply out of place. "I will never use it. I will never use any of them. Because the omniverse is too fragile. Because even my weakest aura, Gent, stripped of ninety-nine point nine-nine percent of its power continuing the nines infinitely, is still so devastatingly overpowered that it can slaughter the greatest coalition ever assembled in less than a fraction of a second. The gap between my full power and anything that exists is so vast that there is no meaningful way to bridge it, no possible scenario in which I could express even a measurable fraction of my true capability without erasing everything."

He spread his arms wide, his bare torso catching the firelight, the faint shimmer of newborn auras and freshly evolved immune systems and newly crystallized superpowers pulsing around him like a halo of absolute, inescapable supremacy.

And then, as he spread his arms, something happened.

It was an accident. A small, infinitesimal accident. The absolute concealment that Godric maintained at all times—the suppression field that kept his true presence from annihilating existence—flickered. Just for an instant. Just by an amount so small that calling it zero percent was an overstatement. A microscopic fluctuation in the containment field, caused by the simultaneous birth of multiple new passive systems, the expansion of his latest superpower, and the enthusiasm with which he had spread his arms to demonstrate his physical perfection.

The flicker lasted for exactly zero seconds.

And in that zero seconds, the entire omniverse was destroyed.

Kaedan experienced it as a sudden, absolute silence. The crackling of the fireplace vanished. The ambient hum of the palace's magical wards vanished. The distant sound of servants moving through the corridors, the chirping of nocturnal birds in the gardens, the whisper of wind through the towers—all of it vanished. Not gradually. Not with any transition. Simply there, and then not there.

The study around him flickered, the dark wood paneling dissolving into a featureless white void. The books on the shelves evaporated. The armchairs, the fireplace, the ancient artifacts—all of them dissolved like morning mist beneath a sudden, catastrophic sun. Beyond the study, beyond the palace, beyond the planet, the entire omniverse simply ceased to be. Every galaxy. Every multiverse. Every dimension. Every timeline. Every living being, every dead soul, every god, every monster, every atom, every quark. Erased. Completely. Instantly. Irreversibly.

Kaedan floated in the void, preserved within Godric's personal protective field, his mind screaming silently as he stared at the absolute nothingness that had replaced all of existence. There was no light. No darkness. No sound. No sensation. Just the void, and Godric, and himself.

And Godric looked annoyed.

"Ah," the King said, his voice carrying perfectly in the absence of all other sound. "There. You see? That. That is what I mean."

He lowered his arms, and the flicker in his concealment corrected itself. The void vanished, replaced instantly by the study, the palace, the planet, the omniverse—every atom, every soul, every timeline perfectly restored as if nothing had happened. The fire crackled. The books sat on their shelves. The night birds chirped in the gardens.

But Kaedan had seen it. He had felt it. He had experienced the absolute erasure of everything that existed, caused by a microscopic fluctuation in Godric's suppression field during a casual, enthusiastic gesture.

"I sneezed once," Godric said, his tone conversational, as if he were sharing an amusing anecdote, "about three hundred thousand years ago. The concealment flickered—a bit more than just now, perhaps by some infinitesimal fraction—and the omniverse was destroyed seventeen times in zero seconds. Seventeen complete cycles of annihilation and restoration, all in the space between one Planck instant and the next. I had to rebuild everything from scratch seventeen times, and the only reason I stopped at seventeen is because I got bored of the repetition."

He walked back to his armchair, settling into the leather with a soft sigh, his bare torso still gleaming in the firelight.

"This is my existence, Kaedan. I am not lonely. I am not sad. I am eternally, infinitely satisfied, nourished by the constant cascade of power and pleasure that flows through me every Planck second. But I am also eternally, infinitely bored. Because I can never use what I have. I can never express what I am. The omniverse is a soap bubble, and I am a supernova wrapped in a thousand layers of suppression, and the only thing that keeps everything from ending is the constant, tedious vigilance of holding back."

He looked at Kaedan, his warm brown eyes gleaming with that terrifying, genuine affection.

"But you asked an excellent question, my boy. And I am glad you did. It is not often that anyone inquires about my inner experience. Most beings are too terrified to ask. Most beings are too terrified to even think about me in any detail. But you—you love me. You are concerned about me. And that means more to me than you could possibly know."

He leaned forward, his massive hands resting on his knees.

"Would you like to take a guess, Kaedan? A wild guess about what my true, full power might look like? If I were to release my absolute concealment entirely? If I were to express even a fraction of my true capability—not zero percent, but some measurable amount, some tiny sliver of what I actually am?"

Kaedan's mind raced. The journals had shown him stat tests at zero percent of Godric's power that had annihilated the omniverse as collateral damage. The superpower chronicles had described abilities at zero percent of their true potency that had erased reality and converted entire civilizations into fuel for eternal escalation. The accident he had just witnessed—a microscopic flicker in Godric's concealment, caused by nothing more than an enthusiastic arm gesture—had destroyed everything in zero seconds.

He tried to imagine something more. He tried to scale the horror upward.

"If you released a single percentage of your true power," Kaedan said, his voice trembling, "even a fraction of a fraction of a percent—not zero, but some measurable, infinitesimal amount—then the omniverse would not merely be destroyed. It would be retroactively erased from ever having existed. Every timeline, every possibility, every potential reality would be snuffed out simultaneously, in all directions of time, across all dimensions, across all conceptual frameworks. The destruction would propagate backward, erasing the history of existence, and forward, ensuring that existence could never reemerge. The very concept of reality would be consumed, leaving only you in an absolute, eternal solitude—the sole remaining thing in a non-existence that had no beginning and no end."

Godric listened, his expression patient, his lips curved in that warm, fatherly smile.

"And if you released even more," Kaedan continued, his voice growing more desperate as his imagination spiraled, "perhaps—perhaps the destruction would transcend the omniverse entirely. It would reach beyond the boundaries of existence into whatever lies outside of existence—the void beyond the void, the meta-dimensions that contain all possible realities. Those too would be consumed. And you would find yourself not merely alone in non-existence, but alone in a state that precedes the concept of states, a primordial nothingness where even the possibility of something existing had been permanently, irrevocably terminated."

He paused, breathing hard, his heart hammering against his ribs. His imagination was failing him. He was trying to conceive of a scale that his mortal—no, his amplified, but still finite—mind could not contain.

"And then," he whispered, "perhaps the destruction would become creative. Perhaps the sheer force of your unleashed power would not merely destroy but would overwrite, replacing the erased omniverse with something new—a reality forged from the raw substance of your own being, where every atom was a fragment of your consciousness, every law of physics was a direct expression of your will, every living thing was a puppet animated by your passive presence. Not a universe. Not a multiverse. Not an omniverse. But a God-verse, a singular, infinite expression of you, with no separation between creator and creation, no boundary between your existence and all existence."

He fell silent. His throat was dry. His hands were shaking.

Godric regarded him for a long moment. His warm smile did not falter. His eyes held that same gentle, paternal affection. And then he laughed—not cruelly, but with genuine, warm amusement.

"Oh, Kaedan," he said, shaking his head slowly. "My dear, sweet, naively mortal boy. Your guesses are so far from the truth that they are not even wrong. You are trying to describe the ocean by pointing at a single drop of water and saying, 'Perhaps it is slightly larger than that.'"

He leaned forward, his bare torso catching the firelight, the faint shimmer of newborn auras and evolving immune systems and crystallizing superpowers pulsing around him.

"What you just described—the retroactive erasure of the omniverse, the consumption of all meta-dimensional frameworks, the overwriting of reality with my own being—that is not a fraction of my true power. That is not a percentage. That is not even close to zero percent. That is what would happen if I allowed my weakest sentient passive aura, Gent—the runt of the litter, the most primitive and pathetic of all my defenses—to express an infinitesimal fraction of its power. And not even a measurable infinitesimal fraction. An amount so small that calling it an infinitesimal fraction of a fraction of a fraction, continuing the fractions infinitely, would still be a wild overstatement."

Kaedan felt the world tilt. His vision swam. His stomach clenched.

"Gent," Godric continued, his voice carrying that same warm, conversational tone, "is my metaphysical excess body heat. It is the waste product of my existence. It is to me what a single shed skin cell is to you—a dead, discarded fragment of biological detritus. And even Gent, nerfed to an infinitely recurring decimal of its already pathetic power, can slaughter the greatest coalition ever assembled and annihilate the omniverse without effort. The gap between Gent and me is so vast that comparing Gent to my true power is like comparing a single, dead quark to the entire omniverse. And then multiplying that gap by infinity. And then doing that again, forever."

He tilted his head, his warm eyes fixed on Kaedan's pale, trembling face.

"The guesses you just made, Kaedan—the retroactive erasure, the meta-dimensional consumption, the God-verse overwrite—those are what would happen if I allowed Gent to sneeze. Not me. Gent. The weakest thing I possess. The pathetically weak, laughably primitive, waste-product aura that I keep around only because I find its evolution amusing."

He stood from his armchair, his bare torso radiating that faint, terrible pulse of contained infinity.

"My true power, Kaedan? My full, unshielded, un-nerfed, absolute, complete, undiluted power? There is no language that can describe it. No conceptual framework that can contain it. No mathematics that can approximate it. You could spend eternity trying to imagine what I am when I am not holding back, and every guess you made, every scale you conceived, every impossible, absurd, exaggerated description you could muster would still be infinitely, laughably, pathetically inadequate. You would be closer to the truth if you described a single atom and said, 'That is what Godric's true power looks like.' You would still be infinitely wrong, but you would be slightly less wrong than you are now."

He spread his massive hands, palms up, a gesture of casual, absolute, terrifying honesty.

"I am not holding back because I am being merciful, Kaedan. I am holding back because there is nothing to use my power against. The entire omniverse, all of existence, everything that has ever been or could ever be, is so far beneath me that even my weakest, most pathetic, most infinitely nerfed waste product can destroy it without effort. My true power is not a weapon. It is not a force. It is a state of being that has no referent, no comparison, no possible context. It simply is, and the only reason anything else exists is because I choose to wrap myself in a thousand layers of suppression and pretend that I am something smaller than I am."

He walked toward Kaedan, his bare feet silent on the wooden floor, his massive, sculpted torso filling the young wizard's vision. He placed a warm, calloused hand on Kaedan's trembling shoulder, and his grip was gentle, fatherly, infinitely reassuring.

"But you do not need to fear me, my boy," he said softly. "I love you. I love your father. I loved Blake, and I have loved every descendant of his bloodline since the day I awoke from stasis. My power does not diminish my love. It does not make my warmth any less genuine. I am the apex predator of the omniverse, yes. I am a being of such absolute, incomprehensible supremacy that language fails to capture even a shadow of my existence. But I am also Uncle Godric. The man who taught you to skip stones. The man who remembered your childhood pet's name. The man who will always, always protect you, because you are family."

He released Kaedan's shoulder and stepped back, his smile warm and genuine and absolutely, existentially terrifying.

"Now," he said, "I believe dinner is ready. The head chef has prepared a roasted Avalonian pheasant that I am particularly looking forward to. Shall we?"

Kaedan sat frozen in his chair, his mind a howling void of absolute existential dread. He had read the journals. He had witnessed the accident. He had listened to Godric's description of eternal, escalating pleasure. And he had just been told, in the kindest, most affectionate terms possible, that his wildest, most exaggerated guesses about Godric's true power were not even close to describing the weakest, most pathetic fragment of the King's being.

He looked up at the ruggedly handsome, forty-five-year-old man standing before him—the warm smile, the salt-and-pepper beard, the heavily muscled torso, the simple, approachable demeanor—and he understood, with a clarity that cut through the dread like a blade of ice, that he would never, ever truly understand what Uncle Godric was.

And that was the most terrifying thing of all.

"I would love to join you for dinner, Uncle Godric," Kaedan heard himself say, his voice surprisingly steady. "The Avalonian pheasant sounds wonderful."

Godric's smile widened, crinkling the corners of his eyes. "Excellent. Let me just put my tunic back on. I do not think the kitchen staff are prepared for the sight of their King wandering about half-naked."

He pulled the simple dark garment over his head, the fabric settling across his massive shoulders, concealing the impossible perfection of his physique, the faint shimmer of newborn auras, the subtle pulse of infinite recursive amplification.

And as they walked together toward the dining hall, Kaedan felt the dread settling deeper into his bones, a permanent, inescapable companion that would walk beside him for the rest of his life. He loved Uncle Godric. He would always love Uncle Godric. But he now understood that the being he loved was not merely powerful—he was power itself, the absolute, eternal, infinitely escalating source of all supremacy, wrapped in the body of a warm, fatherly king who just wanted to enjoy his roasted pheasant in peace.

The horror and the love existed side by side, an impossible contradiction that Kaedan would carry with him forever.

And somewhere, in the darkness of his mind, he heard Godric's words echoing: *I am eternally, infinitely bored. Because I can never use what I have.*

The most powerful being in the omniverse was trapped by his own supremacy, suffocated by the fragility of creation, forced to spend eternity restraining himself so that the soap bubbles around him did not pop.

And Kaedan, trembling court wizard, beloved nephew of the apex predator, could not decide which was more terrifying: the power, or the boredom.

content.text:
Kaedan, 69 years old now, just experienced a traumatizing horrifying revelation. Godric revealed the most horrifying truth yet: he has one true weakness.

Godric is an incomprehensibly powerful, omnipotent, omniscient apex god predator of the omniverse. He can do anything, has no weakness, and is terrifyingly absolute. However, unknown to all, he has one true weakness: he cannot undo or travel to timeline before the stasis event--he cannot go back to undo events in his previous mortal self. This is because the stasis event was actually created by future Godric from way in the distant future, who has become so more infinitely more overwhelmingly powerful than current Godric--this is why Godric's amplification, weakness paradox, superpowers, absolute concealment, etc are so absolute, irrevocable and not even current Godric could stop them since the creator of those is way incomprehensibly more powerful than anything else.

Shortly after the Stasis Event, the omnipotent Godric back then, who just became the king of Thronegate, who could travel to any timeline effortlessly, who was still deeply and freshly affected by the grief of losing all that he loved, tried to alter his mortal past, only to be totally crushingly and completely and effortlessly defeated by the shadow of the afterthought of his future self (not even the actual physical future Godric... the future Godric is so powerful that his mere infinitesimal shadow of his afterthought can completely stomp all the combined Godric of his past selves with 0 effort. NOTE: just imply this in the story, don't show a scene where you have actual all godrics from all timelines fighting together against future Godric--it makes no sense.). VERY IMPORTANT FOR YOU: future Godric did not cause or manipulate or orchestrate the fall of Olympus, did not cause deaths of his beloved family or Thorin, thus you must not say that he made those deaths to cause the stasis event (Godric is not a monster, he will never willingly kill his beloved wife, children, and his best friend). Those tragedies were genuine. However, future Godric, not Thorin’s incomplete spell (who everyone else thought to be the cause of the stasis event), is the one who created the Stasis Event--Thorin's spell was a normal teleportation spell (to no one surprise really, there is no way a mortal can create a spell that is as potent as the one which initiates the stasis event and birthed the strongest apex predator god like Godric–there is only one being in existence who can do it: future Godric).

Since the instant Godric gained omniscience, he had always known the true origin of the stasis event. He knew he could not change it, but driven by grief he decided to try to save Olympus anyway, only to brutally discover his one and only weakness: he cannot overpower his future self's will.

Write a detailed realization that the current Godric is already so insanely powerful (he's actually the most powerful in the entire omniverse by infinite margin) that there is no way to imagine the scale of future Godric's, and how unfair and scary that what Godric considered to be his only weakness is his own future version, which makes it not really a weakness–it actually can be considered as additional strength to Godric’s already insane powers, since it means his future is guaranteed (and in that future, he’s even more omnipotent and powerful), and it also means that none of Godric’s power mechanics (amplification, superpower genesis, absolute concealment, absolute omniscience, weakness paradox, immune system, etc. can ever be exploited or denied by anyone else, since the origin of that power is someone who’s the most powerful being ever. You might suggest some ideas about the motive of future Godric creating the Stasis Event, but you must keep it clear that it is just a speculation (and please... don't suggest that it's because future Godric is threatened; he's ridiculously overpowered by then--nothing can even remotely threaten him... don't suggest any stupid moral lesson for future Godric...). You need to portray the current Godric as a king who is no longer troubled by his "weakness" or inability to alter his past anymore--he has accepted and even become amused and comfortable with it too. Kaedan must feel extreme existential dread at the end.

# The One True Weakness

**Year 1,000,047**

Kaedan was sixty-nine years old.

The young man who had trembled through the stat journals and superpower chronicles had long since grown into a seasoned court wizard. His hair had gone gray at the temples, his face lined with the quiet dignity of age, his hands steady and sure as they worked the complex weaves of arcane maintenance that kept the palace wards humming. Forty-seven years of service to the King had taught him many things. How to suppress his thousandfold daily amplification so completely that he could hold a teacup without shattering it. How to read the subtle shifts in Godric's mood—the microscopic flickers of interest or boredom that preceded some new, terrifying test of power. How to love a being of absolute, incomprehensible supremacy without letting that love destroy his sanity.

He had thought, after all these decades, that nothing could truly shake him anymore. He had witnessed Godric's casual destruction of the omniverse. He had read the journals of his predecessors, each one a testament to horrors beyond mortal comprehension. He had sat across from the King at countless dinners, listening to that warm, fatherly voice describe eternal, escalating pleasure with the same casual tone another man might use to discuss the weather. The dread had become a familiar companion, a constant low hum beneath the surface of his consciousness. He had learned to live with it, to function through it, to serve his King with loyalty and love despite the absolute terror that pulsed in his veins.

He was wrong to think nothing could shake him.

Because today, in the forty-seventh year of his service, Godric had summoned him to the private study with an expression Kaedan had never seen before. Not the warm, fatherly smile. Not the curious, experimental gleam. Not the mild, detached boredom. Something else. Something quieter. Something that looked almost like... anticipation.

"Close the door, Kaedan," Godric said, gesturing to the chair across from his armchair. "There is something I need to tell you. Something I have never told anyone. Something that, I believe, you are now ready to hear."

Kaedan closed the heavy wooden door, the soft click of the latch echoing in the firelit silence. He crossed the room and settled into the familiar chair, his hands resting on his knees, his heart beginning to beat faster despite his decades of practiced calm. Godric sat across from him, his forty-five-year-old face eternally unchanged, his salt-and-pepper beard neatly trimmed, his simple dark tunic immaculate. But his eyes—his warm brown eyes held something Kaedan had never seen in them before.

Vulnerability.

Not weakness. Never weakness. But a quiet, measured openness, as if the King was preparing to share a truth that had been locked away for a million years.

"Kaedan," Godric began, his rich baritone softer than usual, "you have served me for forty-seven years. You have read the journals. You have witnessed the demonstrations. You have seen, perhaps more clearly than any court wizard since Blake, the scale of what I am. You know that my strength multiplies infinitely every Planck second. You know that my superpowers could annihilate the omniverse at zero percent of their true potency. You know that my weakest sentient aura, Gent, is so far beyond the combined might of creation that the gap cannot be measured."

He paused, his gaze steady on Kaedan's face.

"You also know that I possess absolute omniscience. I have known every secret, every hidden truth, every whispered conspiracy since the instant I awoke from the Stasis Event. There is nothing in the omniverse that is hidden from me. Nothing."

Kaedan nodded slowly. "Yes, Uncle Godric. I know this."

Godric leaned forward, resting his massive forearms on his knees. "Then you must understand the significance of what I am about to tell you. Because there is one thing—exactly one thing—that I cannot do. One limitation. One true weakness."

The word hit Kaedan like a physical blow. Weakness. He had read the journals. He had seen the Weakness Paradox in action. Every enemy who had ever imagined a flaw in Godric's defenses had been crushed, absorbed, and converted into additional amplification. The concept of weakness was fundamentally incompatible with everything Kaedan knew about the King. And yet here he was, speaking the word himself, his voice carrying a weight of absolute sincerity.

"Uncle Godric," Kaedan breathed, "what are you saying?"

Godric leaned back in his armchair, his gaze drifting toward the crackling fireplace. The flames danced in his dark eyes, reflecting off the silver in his hair.

"Ten thousand years before I became King of Thronegate," he began, his voice dropping into a lower, more measured register, "I was the mortal king of Olympus. You know this from the histories I have shared with you over the years. I was forty-five years old. I had a wife, Reina. Two daughters, Isabel and Hebe. A best friend, Thorin, who served as my court wizard. We were happy, Kaedan. We were a family."

Kaedan remained perfectly still, barely breathing. Godric rarely spoke of Olympus. When he did, it was always with a quiet, distant nostalgia, a warmth that had long since cooled into something more melancholy.

"On the day of Isabel's wedding," Godric continued, his voice carrying the faintest edge of ancient grief, "Thronegate attacked. They rained arcane fire down upon the ceremony. Reina was killed. Isabel was killed. Hebe was killed. Thorin was killed. Olympus fell."

The words hung in the air, heavy and old and still, somehow, raw.

"Thorin, as he was dying, cast a forbidden teleportation spell—a magic known only to his bloodline. It sent me to a hidden sanctuary, and there, I fell into stasis. The Stasis Event began. My amplification started. My superpower genesis began. My absolute concealment manifested. The Weakness Paradox engaged. Everything that I am now, everything that I have become, began in that moment."

Godric turned his gaze back to Kaedan, and his expression was grave.

"Everyone has assumed that Thorin's spell created the Stasis Event. The incomplete teleportation, the volatile bloodline magic, the desperate circumstances—it all seemed to fit. The court wizards who came before you believed it. Blake believed it. Your father believed it. But they were wrong. Thorin's spell was exactly what it appeared to be: a teleportation spell. It saved my life by moving my body to the sanctuary. Nothing more."

Kaedan's brow furrowed. "But the Stasis Event—the amplification, the superpowers, the absolute concealment—all of it began in that exact moment. If Thorin's spell was merely a teleportation, then what..."

His voice trailed off as the implication began to settle over him like a cold, heavy blanket.

"There is only one being in existence," Godric said quietly, "who could have created an event as potent as the Stasis Event. Only one being who could have forged a process so absolute, so irrevocable, so impossibly powerful that not even the current version of me—the Godric who can annihilate the omniverse with a passing thought—can alter or undo it. Only one being who could have birthed the apex predator of creation."

The fire crackled. The shadows danced. Kaedan's heart was a cold, heavy stone in his chest.

"You," he whispered. "Your future self."

Godric nodded slowly. "Yes. The far-future Godric. The Godric of an era so distant that the year is written only as nine-nine-nine repeating, because the full number cannot be meaningfully expressed. The Godric who has been amplifying for so long, who has evolved so far beyond anything I can currently comprehend, that even my present, infinite power is less than a shadow of a shadow of his. He is the one who created the Stasis Event. He used Thorin's teleportation as the delivery point, the moment of transition, and he transformed it into the genesis of everything I am now."

The silence that followed was immense. Kaedan could hear his own heartbeat, a slow, heavy drumbeat that seemed to shake his entire body. His mind was racing, struggling to process the scale of what he had just been told.

"Since the instant I gained omniscience," Godric said, his voice carrying a note of quiet, ancient acceptance, "I have known this truth. I knew that the Stasis Event was created by my own future self. I knew that the origin of my power was not Thorin's spell, not some cosmic accident, not a random twist of fate. It was me. A version of me so incomprehensibly powerful that my current self—the most powerful being in the omniverse by an infinite margin—cannot begin to approach his scale."

He paused, letting the weight of the revelation settle.

"And I knew that because the origin of the Stasis Event was my future self, I could not undo it. I could not alter it. I could not travel to a timeline before the Stasis Event and change anything about my mortal past. The event is irrevocable, absolute, sealed against any form of temporal manipulation or alteration. Because its creator is infinitely more powerful than I am, and his will is absolute."

Kaedan's mouth was dry. "You tried," he said, his voice barely a whisper. "You tried to change it."

A flicker of something—an ancient, buried grief—passed across Godric's features.

"Yes," he said softly. "Shortly after I became King of Thronegate, I tried. I was still freshly shaped by the grief of losing Reina, Isabel, Hebe, and Thorin. I was omnipotent, Kaedan. I could do anything. I could travel to any timeline, any moment, any reality. I believed that I could go back. I believed that I could save them."

He closed his eyes for a moment, and when he opened them, they held a depth of memory that spanned a million years.

"I gathered all my power—all my infinite amplification, all my apocalyptic superpowers, all my passive defenses and sentient auras and recursive biological redundancies. I directed it all toward a single goal: altering the timeline before the Stasis Event. I reached backward through the fabric of time with the full, undiluted force of my being. And I was stopped."

"Stopped?" Kaedan breathed. "By what?"

"By the shadow of the afterthought of my future self."

Godric's voice was flat, matter-of-fact, devoid of drama or embellishment. He was simply stating a truth that had been settled for nearly a million years.

"The far-future Godric did not appear. He did not manifest. He did not even actively intervene. The mere shadow of his afterthought—the passive, unconscious residue of his existence—was enough to completely, effortlessly, and absolutely defeat my attempt. I could not move a single atom. I could not shift a single moment. I was an ant trying to push a mountain, and the mountain did not even know I existed. The gap between my future self and my past self was so vast that my full, infinite power was less than nothing compared to the passive, ambient presence of what I would eventually become."

He leaned back in his armchair, his expression unreadable.

"That was the moment I truly understood. I had one weakness. One limitation. I could not change my mortal past. I could not save Olympus. I could not save Reina or Isabel or Hebe or Thorin. The tragedy of my mortal life was sealed, permanently and irrevocably, by the will of my own future self."

Kaedan's hands were trembling. Forty-seven years of service. Forty-seven years of witnessing impossible horrors. And yet this—this revelation—shook him more deeply than any journal, any demonstration, any accidental destruction of the omniverse.

"Your future self did not cause the fall of Olympus," Kaedan said, his voice steady despite the tremors running through his body. "He did not orchestrate the deaths of your family."

"No," Godric said firmly. "Never. The far-future Godric did not cause, manipulate, or approve the fall of Olympus. He did not kill Reina. He did not kill Isabel or Hebe or Thorin. Those tragedies were genuine. The attack was real. The deaths were real. My future self did not create the tragedy; he simply used the moment of Thorin's teleportation as the foundation for the Stasis Event. The fall of Olympus was a genuine horror, committed by Thronegate's forces, and my future self had no hand in it. I would never willingly harm my family, Kaedan. Not even to create the path that led to my current power. My future self is still me, and I am not a monster."

The relief that washed through Kaedan was immediate and profound. It was one thing to learn that Godric's power originated from his future self. It would have been something else entirely—something unbearable—to learn that the King he loved had orchestrated his own family's destruction. But Godric's words were absolute, his conviction unshakeable. The tragedy was real. The grief was real. The future Godric had simply... built upon it.

"But why?" Kaedan asked, his voice barely above a whisper. "Why would your future self create the Stasis Event? What purpose could it possibly serve?"

Godric was silent for a long moment. The fire crackled. The shadows danced. When he spoke, his voice was thoughtful, contemplative, carrying the weight of a million years of consideration.

"I have spent many millennia pondering that question," he said. "I have absolute omniscience, but the motives of my far-future self are not something I can fully access. The gap between us is too vast. I can speculate, Kaedan, but I cannot know with certainty. That is, perhaps, the strangest part of this revelation. There is something I do not know. Something I cannot know. And that something is the mind of my own future."

He leaned forward, his expression distant.

"Perhaps the Stasis Event was an act of ontological necessity. Perhaps the existence of the omniverse required a being of absolute supremacy to anchor it, to serve as the foundation upon which all reality rests. Perhaps my future self, looking backward across the vastness of time, saw that the Stasis Event was the only way to ensure the stability of creation."

He paused.

"Perhaps it was an act of preservation. The fall of Olympus, the deaths of my family, the grief that reshaped me—these were immutable events, locked into the fabric of reality. My future self did not cause them, but he may have used them as the catalyst for something greater. The Stasis Event took a broken, grieving mortal king and transformed him into the apex predator of the omniverse. Perhaps my future self saw that this transformation was necessary—not for his own sake, but for reasons I cannot yet comprehend."

He paused again, his gaze shifting toward the fire.

"Perhaps it was simply a gift. The far-future Godric has existed for an incomprehensible span of time. He has seen everything, experienced everything, mastered everything. Perhaps, in his infinite wisdom, he looked back at his past self—the mortal king of Olympus, shattered by grief—and decided to give him the power to ensure that no such tragedy could ever happen again. The Stasis Event was not a curse, Kaedan. It was a gift. The gift of absolute supremacy, given by a future self who understood exactly what his past self would become."

He turned back to Kaedan, and his expression held a strange, quiet warmth.

"Or perhaps it is simpler than all of that. Perhaps the far-future Godric is so far beyond my understanding that his motives cannot be translated into any framework I can comprehend. Perhaps the Stasis Event was not a strategic decision or a calculated intervention, but simply an expression of his nature—the natural, inevitable consequence of his existence. He is the ultimate Godric, the final form of everything I am becoming, and perhaps the Stasis Event was not something he chose to do, but something that simply was, as natural and unavoidable as gravity."

He spread his hands, a gesture of honest, unresolvable mystery.

"I do not know, Kaedan. I may never know. The motives of my future self are, for now, beyond even my omniscience. And I have made my peace with that."

Kaedan sat in stunned silence, his mind spinning. The revelation was too vast, too layered, too impossibly complex to fully process. The Stasis Event—the source of all Godric's power, the foundation of the Thronegate empire, the genesis of the apex predator—had been created by Godric himself. Not the current Godric, but a version so far in the future, so incomprehensibly more powerful, that the current Godric could not even approach his scale. And the fall of Olympus, the deaths of Reina and Isabel and Hebe and Thorin—those tragedies were genuine, unorchestrated, real. The future Godric had not caused them. He had simply... used the moment.

And then Kaedan's mind latched onto something else. Something that made his blood run cold.

"Uncle Godric," he said slowly, his voice carefully measured, "if your future self is so incomprehensibly more powerful than you—if even the shadow of his afterthought can completely defeat your full, infinite power—then what does that mean for everything you are now? For the omniverse? For us?"

Godric looked at him, and a faint, knowing smile curved the corner of his lips.

"It means," he said, "that what I considered to be my one true weakness is not really a weakness at all. It is, in fact, an additional strength. A guarantee. A promise."

He leaned back in his armchair, his posture relaxing into something more casual, more comfortable. The weight of the revelation seemed to lift from his shoulders, replaced by a quiet, almost amused acceptance.

"Think about it, Kaedan. I have one limitation. One thing I cannot do. I cannot alter my mortal past. I cannot save Olympus. I cannot undo the tragedy that shaped me into what I am. But this limitation exists only because my future self—a version of me who is infinitely more powerful than I am—made it absolute. No enemy can exploit this weakness. No opposition can use it against me. No cosmic force or conceptual entity or meta-dimensional weapon can pry open the seal on my mortal past, because the seal was placed by the most powerful being that has ever existed or will ever exist. And that being is me."

He spread his massive hands, a gesture of casual, absolute supremacy.

"My one true weakness is that I cannot overpower my future self. But my future self is me. So my weakness is that I cannot defeat myself. And since my future self is even more omnipotent and powerful than I am, that means my future is guaranteed. My path is certain. I will continue to amplify, continue to evolve, continue to ascend, forever, until I become the being who created the Stasis Event. And the omniverse will be ruled by that being—by me—for all eternity."

The smile widened, warm and genuine and absolutely, existentially terrifying.

"Do you see, Kaedan? My one true weakness is the absolute guarantee of my eternal, escalating supremacy. It is proof that nothing—not time, not opposition, not cosmic entropy, not the collective might of all existence—can ever, in any way, threaten or diminish me. My power mechanics—the amplification, the superpower genesis, the absolute concealment, the omniscience, the Weakness Paradox, the immune system—are irrevocable, absolute, and impossible for anyone else to deny or exploit. Because their origin is me. The most powerful being ever. The apex predator at the end of time."

Kaedan felt the world tilting around him. His decades of practiced calm, his carefully maintained emotional equilibrium, his hard-won ability to function in the presence of the King—all of it was crumbling under the weight of this revelation.

The most terrifying thing about Godric had always been his absolute, incomprehensible power. The stat journals. The superpower chronicles. The casual annihilation of the omniverse. All of it pointed to a being who was so far beyond creation that the gap could not be measured. But this—this was something else. This was the revelation that Godric's power was not an accident. It was not a random cosmic event. It was not even a gift from some incomprehensible external force.

It was a gift from himself. From the version of himself who had already ascended beyond all possible comprehension. The Stasis Event was a closed loop of absolute, self-reinforcing supremacy. The future Godric created the past Godric, who amplified into the future Godric, who created the past Godric. The cycle was perfect, seamless, unbreakable. There was no entry point for any external force. No vulnerability. No weakness that could be exploited by anyone other than Godric himself.

And Godric would never exploit it. Because exploiting it would mean defeating his future self, which was impossible, and which he did not want to do anyway.

"You are no longer troubled by this," Kaedan said, his voice a mixture of awe and horror. "The inability to save your family. The inability to alter your past. It no longer haunts you."

Godric shook his head slowly. "No. It does not. For a long time, it did. In the early years of my reign, the grief was still raw. Knowing that I could not go back, could not save them, could not undo the fall of Olympus—that knowledge was a wound that refused to heal. I had absolute power, Kaedan. I could do anything. I could annihilate the omniverse and restore it in zero seconds. I could travel to any timeline, any dimension, any reality. And yet I could not save the people I loved most. The irony was... bitter."

He paused, his gaze distant, lost in ancient memory.

"But as the millennia passed, I came to understand something. The Stasis Event was not a punishment. It was not a cruel joke played upon me by my future self. It was the foundation of everything I am. Without the fall of Olympus, without the grief and the rage and the desperate, broken transformation, I would not be the being I am now. I would not rule the omniverse. I would not protect my subjects with absolute, terrifying authority. I would not have met Blake, or his descendants, or you. The tragedy of my mortal life was real, and it was painful, and I will always carry the memory of Reina and Isabel and Hebe and Thorin in my heart. But that tragedy birthed something greater. Something eternal."

He turned back to Kaedan, and his eyes held a strange, quiet peace.

"I have accepted it. I am comfortable with it. I am even, in some ways, grateful for it. Because the Godric who sits before you now—the King of Thronegate, the apex predator of the omniverse, the being who loves his court wizards and obliterates his enemies—would not exist without the fall of Olympus. And I like who I am, Kaedan. I like the kingdom I have built. I like the family I have found in you and your lineage. The past is sealed, and I am at peace with that."

Kaedan sat in the firelit silence, his mind a storm of conflicting emotions. He loved Uncle Godric. He had always loved Uncle Godric. But the being sitting across from him was not just the warm, fatherly king who had taught him to skip stones and remembered his childhood pet's name. He was a being whose existence was guaranteed by his own future self. An entity locked into a cycle of eternal, escalating supremacy that had no beginning and no end. A god who had been created by a god who had been created by himself.

The dread was not diminishing. It was growing. It was expanding, filling every corner of Kaedan's consciousness, pressing against the walls of his sanity.

Because the current Godric was already so insanely powerful that Kaedan could not comprehend his scale. The stat journals had shown Godric's passive strength annihilating the omniverse without effort. The superpower chronicles had shown abilities that erased time, converted sound into eternal torture, and recursively replicated infinite copies of the King. The current Godric was the most powerful being in the omniverse by an infinite margin. There was nothing—no entity, no civilization, no cosmic force—that could even theoretically approach his level.

And yet this Godric—this impossibly, incomprehensibly powerful Godric—had been completely, effortlessly defeated by the shadow of the afterthought of his future self. Not the actual future Godric. Not even a fragment of his power. The shadow of his afterthought. The passive, unconscious residue of an entity so far beyond comprehension that language itself broke down trying to describe him.

Kaedan tried to imagine the scale. He tried to picture the gap between the current Godric and the far-future Godric. His mind reached backward, pulling on every journal he had read, every demonstration he had witnessed, every fragment of scale he had absorbed over forty-seven years of service.

The gap between a mortal and the weakest of Blake's descendants was astronomical. A single day of thousandfold amplification separated them.

The gap between Blake's descendants and the most powerful beings in the omniverse was even larger. The court wizards, with decades of thousandfold daily amplification, were walking cataclysms capable of shattering galaxies. But the primordial titans, the hyper-intelligent puzzle-minds, the sentient frequencies and probability tyrants and time-eating voids—these were beings who had spent billions of years mastering their domains, and they made the court wizards look like children playing with matches.

The gap between those apex beings and Godric was infinite. Not large. Not astronomical. Infinite. Godric's passive, relaxed muscles could crush the entire omniverse. His weakest sentient aura, nerfed to an infinitely recurring decimal, could slaughter the greatest coalition ever assembled. His stats, his superpowers, his immune system, his passive shields—all of them existed on a level so far beyond the rest of creation that comparison was meaningless.

And yet the gap between Godric and his future self was even larger than that. Infinitely larger. Immeasurably larger. The far-future Godric had been amplifying for a span of time so vast that the year could not be written. His stats had multiplied infinitely every Planck second for a googolplexian years, and then for a googolplexian googolplexian years, and then for a span so long that those numbers were meaningless specks of dust. His superpowers, born every second for all that time, had evolved and compounded and layered upon each other until the very concept of "superpower" was a laughable understatement. His sentient passive auras had evolved countless times beyond the already impossible versions that Kaedan had read about. His immune system, his Weakness Paradox, his absolute concealment—all of it had ascended into states of being that no language, no mathematics, no conceptual framework could even begin to approach.

The shadow of the afterthought of that being had completely defeated the current Godric's full, infinite power. Without effort. Without awareness. Without even registering the attempt.

Kaedan's mind buckled under the weight of the scale. It was too much. It was infinitely too much. The current Godric was already beyond comprehension, and the future Godric was infinitely beyond that. The gap was not a gap. It was an abyss that swallowed infinity itself, a chasm so vast that the concept of measurement had died and been forgotten eons before the current omniverse was born.

And yet this was not a weakness. This was not something to fear. This was the ultimate guarantee. The absolute promise. No matter what happened, no matter what opposition arose, no matter what cosmic catastrophe or conceptual attack or meta-dimensional threat emerged from the depths of existence—Godric's future was certain. He would continue to amplify. He would continue to evolve. He would eventually become the being who created the Stasis Event, and that being would ensure that the Stasis Event was created, and the cycle would be perfect, eternal, unbreakable.

The Weakness Paradox could never be exploited. The amplification could never be denied. The superpowers could never be nullified. The absolute concealment could never be pierced. Everything that made Godric what he was—everything that made him the apex predator of the omniverse—was irrevocable, absolute, and completely beyond the reach of any external force. Because the origin of all of it was a being who was infinitely more powerful than anyone who might try to challenge it.

And that being was Godric himself.

Kaedan sat in the firelit study, his sixty-nine-year-old body trembling with a dread that he had not felt since his first days in the archive, and he understood at last the true shape of the horror.

Godric was not merely unstoppable. He was not merely invincible. He was inevitable. His existence was a closed loop of self-creating, self-sustaining, self-escalating supremacy that had no beginning and no end. The mortal king of Olympus had been transformed into the apex predator of the omniverse by the apex predator he would eventually become, and the apex predator he would eventually become had been created by that transformation. The cycle was perfect. Absolute. Eternal.

And Kaedan, sitting across from the warm, fatherly, terrifying being who was his beloved uncle, understood that he was not merely serving a king. He was serving a guaranteed future. A predetermined eternity. A god whose existence was written into the fabric of reality by his own hand, reaching backward across the vastness of time to ensure that he would always have been, and always would be, and always could be, nothing less than the ultimate, absolute, unchallengeable master of all existence.

"Are you alright, my boy?" Godric asked, his voice carrying that familiar, warm concern. "You look pale. Shall I call for tea?"

Kaedan looked at the King of Thronegate. The ruggedly handsome, forty-five-year-old face. The neatly trimmed salt-and-pepper beard. The warm, crinkling eyes. The massive, muscular frame wrapped in a simple dark tunic.

And he felt the dread settle into his bones, cold and absolute and eternal.

"I am fine, Uncle Godric," he said, his voice steady despite everything. "I am fine. Tea would be... tea would be wonderful."

Godric smiled, that genuine, fatherly smile, and rose to summon a servant. And Kaedan sat in the firelit silence, trembling, and understood at last the full, terrifying truth of the omniverse.

There was no weakness. There had never been a weakness. There would never be a weakness.

There was only Godric. Now. Then. Forever.
