# The Tourist

**One Day Before the Attack**

Roth was reviewing the latest thaumic harvest reports when Godric poked his head around the doorframe of the court wizard's study with the expression of a man who had just invented a new and particularly delightful form of mischief. This was, in Roth's thirty-seven years of service, the most terrifying expression the King could wear. It meant something absurd was about to happen, and Roth would be expected to participate, and by the end of it his understanding of reality would have been violently rearranged in ways that would require months of silent contemplation to process.

"Roth, my boy," Godric said, his rich baritone warm with barely contained enthusiasm, "cancel your afternoon appointments. We are going on an excursion."

Roth set down his quill with the careful, deliberate motion of a man who knew that any sudden movement might shatter the fragile calm of the moment. "An excursion, Your Majesty?"

"Yes. A visit. A little trip. I have decided to engage in some tourism." Godric stepped fully into the room, and Roth saw that he was carrying a small satchel over one massively muscled shoulder. The King was dressed in his usual simple dark tunic, his salt-and-pepper hair neatly combed, his ruggedly handsome forty-five-year-old face alight with a boyish excitement that would have been charming on anyone else. On Godric, it was a harbinger of cosmic catastrophe.

"The largest resistance coalition ever assembled," Godric continued, settling into the armchair across from Roth's desk with the casual ease of a man discussing weekend plans, "is scheduled to launch their ultimate attack against me tomorrow. They have been preparing for approximately four thousand, six hundred and twelve years. They believe themselves completely hidden from my perception. They have constructed a weapon they call the Absolute Annulment Cannon, which is designed to fire a concentrated beam of conceptual negation at my physical form, erasing me from existence at the fundamental level of reality. They are very proud of it."

Roth's blood turned to ice water. "Your Majesty, if they are hidden, how do you—"

Godric waved a dismissive hand. "Absolute omniscience, Roth. I have known about their little project since the first microsecond of its conception. I have watched them build it, piece by piece, argument by argument, desperate hope by desperate hope. The only reason they still exist is because I was curious. I wanted to see what the greatest minds in the resistance could come up with when given four millennia and absolutely no interference. It has been mildly entertaining, like watching a particularly ambitious colony of ants construct a hill."

He leaned forward, his warm brown eyes gleaming. "Their attack is tomorrow. Today, I thought it would be fun to pay them a visit. A surprise inspection, if you will. And you, my dear Roth, are going to accompany me."

Roth's mouth opened, closed, opened again. A faint ringing had started in his ears. "Your Majesty, you want to visit the headquarters of the largest resistance coalition in omniversal history, one day before they attempt to destroy you, as a form of... tourism?"

"Precisely. I am so glad you understand." Godric reached into his satchel and produced two objects: a false mustache made of cheap synthetic fibers, and a pair of spectacles with thick, exaggerated frames that held no actual lenses. "I have prepared disguises. We would not want to be recognized."

Roth stared at the false mustache. It was a lurid shade of orange, completely mismatched with Godric's salt-and-pepper beard, and it was clearly designed to be affixed with a small dab of adhesive that was already peeling at the edges. The spectacles were the sort of thing a stage actor might wear to indicate that he was playing a scholar, comically oversized and utterly unconvincing.

"Your Majesty," Roth said, his voice very carefully level, "you are the most recognizable being in the omniverse. Your face is on every coin, every statue, every official portrait in every subjugated reality. The salt-and-pepper hair, the beard, the general physical proportions—these are iconic. A false mustache is not going to fool anyone."

"Nonsense," Godric said, affixing the orange mustache to his upper lip with a practiced motion. It sat slightly askew, the synthetic fibers clashing horribly with his natural beard. He put on the spectacles, which magnified his eyes to an unsettling degree. "There. I am now an anonymous traveler. Call me... Grog. Yes, Grog the Merchant. And you can be my assistant, Rothgar."

"Rothgar."

"It is a very convincing disguise, Roth. Stop being so dramatic."

Roth looked at the King of Thronegate, the apex predator of the omniverse, the being whose passive body heat could annihilate creation, sitting in his study with an orange fake mustache and ridiculous glasses, and he felt the familiar sensation of his sanity quietly unspooling.

"I do not have a disguise," Roth said weakly.

Godric reached into the satchel again and produced a floppy felt hat with a wide brim. "This will do nicely. Put it on. We are leaving in thirty seconds."

---

Godric did not teleport them directly into the heart of the resistance base. That, he explained with the air of a connoisseur, would be rude. Instead, he materialized them approximately two kilometers from the outer perimeter, on a rocky outcropping that overlooked the vast, hidden fortress. The base was situated in a pocket dimension accessible only through a series of heavily encrypted dimensional gateways, buried beneath layers of false realities and decoy universes, shielded from every form of magical detection ever conceived.

It was, Roth had to admit, an impressive facility. The fortress sprawled across the equivalent of several thousand square kilometers, a massive complex of gleaming obsidian towers, humming energy conduits, and fortified defensive emplacements. Warships the size of gas giants hung in low orbit, their hulls bristling with weapons that could shatter galaxies. Legions of hyper-augmented soldiers drilled in vast parade grounds, their movements perfectly synchronized, their armor glowing with the contained power of dying stars. At the center of the complex, rising above everything else like a dark finger pointing accusingly at the heavens, was the Absolute Annulment Cannon—a weapon so vast that its barrel alone stretched beyond the local multiversal boundary, its firing mechanism powered by the sacrificed life-forces of a trillion willing martyrs.

"The architecture is quite striking," Godric observed, adjusting his spectacles. "I particularly like the use of obsidian for the primary structures. It gives the whole facility a very dramatic, 'we are serious about destroying the tyrant' aesthetic. Very classic."

Roth's floppy hat drooped over his eyes. He pushed it back with a trembling hand. "Your Majesty, there are approximately seventeen billion soldiers in that base."

"Seventeen billion, three hundred and forty-two million, eight hundred and sixteen thousand, and twelve," Godric corrected. "One of them is currently in the latrine. I will spare you the details."

"I do not think a felt hat is going to conceal my identity from seventeen billion soldiers."

"Have faith, Roth. The disguise is a state of mind."

Godric began walking toward the outer perimeter, his heavy boots crunching on the rocky ground with an easy, unhurried rhythm. Roth, with absolutely no other option, followed. The floppy hat flapped against his ears with every step.

---

The outer perimeter was guarded by a battalion of Void-Shatterer elites, soldiers genetically engineered from the cellular material of extinct primordial titans, clad in armor forged from the compressed corpses of dead universes. They were immense beings, each one standing nearly four meters tall, their bodies radiating an aura of such intense martial supremacy that the ambient space-time around them buckled and warped. Their weapons were singularity rifles, capable of firing miniature black holes at velocities that violated causality.

The lead guard, a hulking brute named Kael-7, spotted the two approaching figures and immediately raised his rifle. His neural processors, augmented with predictive combat algorithms that could analyze a threat across all possible timelines, screamed into high alert.

"Halt!" Kael-7 bellowed, his voice shaking the ground. "This is a restricted sector! Identify yourselves immediately or be atomized!"

Godric stopped walking. He adjusted his orange mustache, which had begun to peel at the left corner, and offered the guard a warm, friendly smile. "Good afternoon, my good man. My name is Grog, and this is my assistant, Rothgar. We are humble merchants from the outer provinces, and we were hoping to tour your impressive facility. We have heard marvelous things about the Absolute Annulment Cannon and simply had to see it for ourselves."

There was a long, frozen moment of silence. The Void-Shatterer guards stared at the two intruders. Roth's floppy hat drooped again. Godric's spectacles magnified his eyes to a disturbing degree. The orange mustache fluttered slightly in the dimensional breeze.

Kael-7's predictive combat algorithms, which had been trained on every possible threat scenario across every possible timeline, processed the visual data and reached a conclusion that caused his neural processors to experience something very close to a seizure.

The intruder's facial structure matched the known appearance of Godric, King of Thronegate, with an accuracy of 99.9999%. The salt-and-pepper hair, the neatly trimmed beard, the ruggedly handsome features, the heavily muscled frame, the general physical proportions—every biometric marker screamed positive identification. The algorithms then processed the orange mustache, the spectacles, and the claim of being a merchant named Grog. The contradiction caused a cascading logic failure that temporarily crashed Kael-7's higher cognitive functions.

"You," Kael-7 managed, his voice suddenly very different from the authoritative bellow of a moment before. "You are... you are..."

"Grog," Godric said helpfully. "Of the Eastern Merchant's Guild. We specialize in artisanal cheeses and handcrafted textiles."

The other guards had raised their weapons by now, their own combat algorithms arriving at the same impossible conclusion. One of them, a female Void-Shatterer named Seris-12, began to tremble so violently that her singularity rifle clattered against her armor.

"Godric," she whispered. "It's Godric. The tyrant. The king. He's here. He's wearing a fake mustache."

"I am Grog," Godric insisted, his tone patient but firm. "I have never met this Godric fellow, though I hear he is very handsome and rules with a firm but just hand. Now, about that tour—"

Kael-7's training overrode his terror. Four thousand years of preparation, four thousand years of drilling for exactly this moment, kicked in with the force of absolute desperation. He raised his singularity rifle and fired.

The miniature black hole erupted from the barrel with a scream of violated physics, a singularity of pure gravitational annihilation that could swallow a galaxy whole. It crossed the distance between Kael-7 and Godric in a Planck instant, its event horizon already expanding to consume the space where the intruder stood.

The black hole touched Godric's chest. And then it simply was not there anymore.

There was no explosion, no flash of light, no gravitational collapse. The singularity, which contained the compressed mass of a billion dead stars, ceased to exist as if it had never been fired. Godric's passive shields—the infinite recursive layers of pre-nullification that had evolved countless times across the googolplexian years—had evaluated the attack, determined that it did not qualify as a threat worth acknowledging, and had deleted it from reality before it could inconvenience their master.

Godric looked down at his chest, where the black hole had briefly been, and then looked up at Kael-7 with a expression of mild, fatherly disappointment.

"That was quite rude," he said. "I am simply trying to arrange a tour. There is no need for violence."

Kael-7 fired again. And again. And again. Every Void-Shatterer in the battalion opened fire simultaneously, a torrent of apocalyptic weaponry that should have annihilated the entire pocket dimension. Singularity rifles, entropy cannons, conceptual erasure beams, temporal displacement warheads—every weapon in their considerable arsenal discharged at the maximum possible rate, a symphony of absolute destruction that had been designed to challenge the apex predator himself.

Every single attack vanished before it could reach Godric's body. Not deflected. Not absorbed. Vanished. The passive shields evaluated each incoming threat, found it wanting, and simply edited it out of the timeline. The guards experienced the unique horror of watching their most powerful weapons disappear into absolute nothingness without causing so much as a ripple in their target's orange mustache.

Roth, standing slightly behind Godric and desperately trying to keep his floppy hat on his head, watched the display with the numb, detached horror of a man who had long since accepted that his life was a series of increasingly absurd catastrophes. The Void-Shatterers were pouring out enough firepower to erase a decillion galaxies, and Godric was patiently waiting for them to finish, his expression that of a tolerant father allowing a child to exhaust a tantrum.

After approximately thirty seconds, the firing stopped. The guards' weapons were depleted, their ammunition stores drained, their reality-bending capacitors completely empty. They stood in stunned silence, staring at the two intruders who had not moved a single step from where they stood.

"Are you quite finished?" Godric asked pleasantly.

Kael-7 fell to his knees. His neural processors, unable to reconcile the absolute failure of every conceivable offensive strategy, simply shut down, and the massive Void-Shatterer collapsed into a catatonic heap on the rocky ground. The other guards followed suit, their minds broken by the sheer impossibility of what they had witnessed.

Godric stepped around their prone forms with the careful courtesy of a man avoiding puddles on a rainy day. "Come along, Rothgar. The main entrance appears to be just ahead."

---

The interior of the resistance base was a study in organized panic. Alarms were screaming, klaxons blaring, emergency protocols activating across every level of the massive complex. The entire facility had detected the skirmish at the outer perimeter, and the seventeen-billion-strong defense force was mobilizing with the desperate, frantic energy of a civilization facing its final moment.

Godric walked through the chaos with the calm, leisurely pace of a tourist admiring the local architecture. He paused periodically to examine points of interest—a particularly well-designed energy conduit, an impressive holographic tactical display, a motivational poster that read "FREEDOM OR OBLIVION" in bold, heroic lettering.

"Look at this, Roth," he said, gesturing toward a massive mural that depicted a heroic figure standing triumphantly over a defeated tyrant. The tyrant bore a striking resemblance to Godric, though the artist had taken some liberties with the facial proportions. "They have depicted me as slightly overweight. I find that hurtful. I have maintained this physique for an incomprehensible number of years."

Roth, whose floppy hat had fallen over one eye, tried to formulate a response but found that his vocabulary had been reduced to a series of strangled, non-committal noises. He was a court wizard, a descendant of Blake, a being whose thousandfold daily amplification made him a walking cataclysm by any reasonable standard. And he was following a fake-mustached god through the heart of an enemy fortress, utterly convinced that he was about to die of sheer existential terror.

Squads of elite soldiers rushed past them, their weapons raised, their sensors screaming with the impossible readings of the intruder's presence. And yet none of them fired. None of them even raised their weapons. Because every soldier in the resistance had been equipped with threat-assessment algorithms, and every single algorithm, when pointed at the casually strolling figure of Godric, returned the same result: a string of error codes and a single, stark message.

TARGET CANNOT BE HARMED. ATTACK IMPOSSIBLE. SURRENDER IMMEDIATELY.

The algorithms were, technically, a function of the Weakness Paradox. Every soldier who had been trained to identify Godric's weaknesses had, in doing so, triggered the paradox, feeding him additional amplification and immunity. The resistance had spent four thousand years sharpening their weapons against the very thing that made those weapons useless. The more they prepared, the more impossible their goal became. And now, at the culmination of their efforts, they were facing the living proof of their absolute, inescapable futility.

---

The central command chamber was a vast, domed space at the heart of the fortress, filled with holographic displays, tactical consoles, and the gathered leadership of the largest resistance coalition in omniversal history. General Varek, a battle-hardened veteran of a thousand cosmic wars, stood at the central command podium, his scarred face pale with a mixture of fury and disbelief. Around him, the council of resistance leaders—representatives of decillions of subjugated civilizations, each one a legendary hero in their own right—stared at the security feeds with expressions of mounting horror.

The main doors of the command chamber, which were rated to withstand the direct impact of a multiversal collapse, swung open with a soft, polite creak. Godric stepped through, his orange mustache now drooping at a tragic angle, his spectacles slightly fogged from the ambient humidity of the base's atmospheric processors. Roth followed behind him, his floppy hat now held in his hands, his face the color of fresh milk.

"Good afternoon, everyone," Godric said, his rich baritone resonating through the stunned silence of the command chamber. "I do hope I am not interrupting anything important. My assistant and I were in the area and simply had to see the famous Absolute Annulment Cannon. The brochures do not do it justice."

General Varek's hand moved toward his sidearm—a conceptual-disruption pistol that could unmake abstract entities—but the movement was automatic, instinctual, completely divorced from any rational assessment of the situation. His tactical mind, trained across millennia of warfare, processed the impossibility of Godric's presence with the same cold, analytical precision that had won him a thousand campaigns.

"You knew," Varek said, his voice barely a whisper. "You knew the entire time."

Godric removed his spectacles and polished them on the sleeve of his tunic, a gesture of such casual mundanity that several of the resistance leaders felt their minds crack under the cognitive dissonance.

"Of course I knew," Godric said. "I have known since the first microsecond you conceived of this endeavor. I watched you select this pocket dimension. I watched you forge the dimensional gateways and bury them beneath the false realities. I watched you recruit your seventeen billion soldiers and train them in anti-Godric combat tactics. I watched you argue about the design of the Absolute Annulment Cannon, which, by the way, has a slight misalignment in the tertiary focusing array that will cause a 0.002% reduction in conceptual negation output. I assume you were planning to fix that before tomorrow's attack."

He smiled, a warm, friendly expression that was absolutely, existentially terrifying.

"I have been very curious to see what you would come up with. Four thousand years of preparation. The combined intellect of the greatest minds in the resistance. The sacrificed life-forces of a trillion willing martyrs. I was genuinely interested to discover if you had found something new. Some conceptual weakness I had not yet encountered. Some angle of attack that might, for even a fraction of a Planck instant, make me feel something."

His expression shifted, the warmth dimming slightly.

"I must confess, I am a little disappointed. The Absolute Annulment Cannon, while impressive in scale, is fundamentally just another brute-force approach. You are trying to erase me from existence by applying overwhelming conceptual negation. It is essentially the same strategy as the Null-Frequency Cannon in Year 89,004, or the Finality Matrix in Year 10,000. You have just made it bigger. More powerful. But the underlying principle is unchanged. You have not discovered anything new."

He spread his massive hands, a gesture of mild, paternal regret.

"I was hoping for something more creative."

The silence in the command chamber was absolute. The resistance leaders—the greatest heroes of the omniverse, the last hope of decillions of subjugated civilizations—sat frozen in their chairs, their minds struggling to process the complete and total invalidation of everything they had worked for.

General Varek's hand finally closed around his sidearm. He drew it, raised it, and fired in a single, fluid motion born of desperation rather than hope. The conceptual-disruption beam, which could unmake abstract entities and shatter the very idea of existence, lanced across the command chamber and struck Godric directly in the center of his chest.

Godric looked down at the point of impact with mild curiosity. The beam was still connected to the pistol, a shimmering conduit of absolute dissolution that should have erased him from the timeline. It was not being nullified. It was not being reflected. It was simply... not working. The conceptual-disruption energy was touching his body and finding no purchase, no vulnerability, no conceptual framework upon which to act. It was like trying to erase the concept of infinity by shouting at it.

"Ah," Godric said. "That is the conceptual-disruption pistol. I gained absolute immunity to conceptual-disruption weaponry approximately seven hundred thousand years ago, when a minor deity in the Outer Reaches imagined that my conceptual stability might be a weakness. The Weakness Paradox triggered before he had finished forming the thought. I have been immune ever since. I am surprised your intelligence reports did not mention that."

He reached up and, with two fingers, gently plucked the beam from his chest as if removing a stray thread. The conceptual-disruption energy, which could unmake reality itself, went out with a faint, apologetic fizzle.

"Would anyone else care to try something?" Godric asked, looking around the command chamber with the polite, expectant air of a teacher waiting for a student to answer a question. "I am happy to wait. We have all day. The attack is not until tomorrow, after all."

No one moved. No one spoke. The silence was so complete that Roth could hear the faint, rhythmic thumping of his own heart, each beat a desperate affirmation that he was still alive, still conscious, still standing in the presence of the apex predator.

"I thought not," Godric said. He turned to Roth, his expression brightening. "Rothgar, would you like to see the cannon up close? We have come all this way. It would be a shame not to take the full tour."

Roth, who had been standing motionless with his floppy hat clutched to his chest, managed to produce a sound that might have been a word. It was not, but Godric took it as assent.

---

The Absolute Annulment Cannon was even more impressive up close. Its barrel stretched upward into the dimensional void, a massive structure of gleaming dark metal and pulsing energy conduits, its firing mechanism a complex web of conceptual resonators and sacrificial martyr-cores. The cannon was designed to channel the willing self-extinction of a trillion souls into a single, concentrated beam of absolute negation—a beam that would, if fired, erase its target from existence at the most fundamental level of reality.

Godric walked around the base of the cannon with the appreciative eye of an engineer examining a well-crafted piece of machinery. He paused to examine a particular energy conduit, traced his finger along the alignment of a focusing array, and nodded slowly.

"The craftsmanship is excellent," he said. "The martyr-core integration is particularly elegant. You have managed to achieve a 99.8% efficiency in conceptual energy transfer, which is genuinely impressive. Most civilizations attempting to build a weapon of this scale top out at 97%. You should be proud of your work."

General Varek, who had followed them to the cannon chamber along with the rest of the council, stared at Godric with the hollow, empty eyes of a man whose entire existence had been rendered meaningless. He had spent four thousand years preparing for this moment. Four thousand years of sacrifice, of struggle, of desperate hope. And the tyrant he had sought to destroy was now complimenting the craftsmanship of his weapon.

"Why?" Varek asked, his voice cracking. "Why did you come here? Why did you let us build this? Why did you let us hope?"

Godric turned to face the general, his expression soft, almost kind.

"Because hope is important," he said. "Because the struggle, even a futile one, gives meaning to existence. I believed, once, that mortal resilience required genuine challenges to overcome. I was wrong about that—the challenges never truly existed—but the belief led me to allow your coalition to persist. I was curious. I wanted to see what you would create. What you would sacrifice. What you would become in the face of impossible odds."

He paused.

"I am not a monster, General. I did not let you hope out of cruelty. I let you hope because I genuinely wanted to see if you could surprise me. If you could find some angle, some strategy, some conceptual framework that I had not already absorbed and mastered and rendered irrelevant. I have been accumulating immunities and masteries for a very long time. I was curious if the combined intellect of the resistance could produce something new."

He looked up at the massive cannon, his expression thoughtful.

"You did not. But you came closer than most. The cannon is a remarkable achievement. In any other context, against any other opponent, it would be an absolute, unstoppable force. You could have conquered the omniverse with this weapon. You could have erased the highest gods and the oldest primordial entities. You could have reshaped reality itself."

He turned back to Varek, and his eyes held a strange, ancient sadness.

"But you were never fighting any other opponent. You were fighting me. And I am not merely powerful. I am the origin of power. Everything that exists, everything that can be conceived, everything that can be imagined—I have already absorbed it, mastered it, and rendered it irrelevant. The cannon you built is a masterpiece of mortal ingenuity. But it cannot harm me. Nothing can harm me. That is not arrogance, General. It is simply the truth."

Varek's legs gave out. He collapsed to his knees on the cold metal floor of the cannon chamber, his scarred face wet with tears he had not realized he was shedding. The other council members stood frozen behind him, their expressions ranging from catatonic disbelief to silent, weeping despair.

"What happens now?" Varek whispered. "What do we do?"

Godric considered the question for a long moment. Then he shrugged, a casual roll of his massive shoulders.

"Whatever you like. I am not here to destroy you. I am not here to punish you. I am here because I was curious, and because I wanted to see the cannon up close before I inevitably have to disable it tomorrow. You are still free to launch your attack as planned. I will be waiting. I will even let the cannon fire—I am curious to see the beam in action. The visuals are probably quite spectacular."

He reached out and placed a warm, calloused hand on Varek's shoulder. The gesture was gentle, fatherly, infinitely reassuring.

"Take tonight to rest. To reflect. To spend time with your comrades. Tomorrow, you will do what you feel you must do. I will not hold your resistance against you. I never have. The only reason any of you still exist is because I allowed it, and I do not withdraw that permission now."

He removed his hand and stepped back, his expression shifting to something almost cheerful.

"Now, Rothgar and I should be going. We have a dinner reservation at the palace, and the Nourisher gets terribly anxious when I am late. She has prepared a new caramelized root vegetable glaze that I am quite eager to try."

He adjusted his orange mustache, which had now peeled almost completely off and was hanging by a single thread of adhesive, and offered the assembled resistance leaders a warm, friendly smile.

"It was a pleasure visiting your facility. Truly. The architecture is striking, the cannon is impressive, and your soldiers are very dedicated. You should be proud of what you have built, even if it cannot accomplish its intended purpose. There is honor in the attempt."

He turned to Roth. "Come along, Rothgar. We should not keep the Nourisher waiting."

Roth, who had been standing in silent, trembling horror for the entirety of the conversation, managed to nod. He placed his floppy hat back on his head, where it immediately drooped over his eyes, and followed Godric toward the exit.

Behind them, the resistance leaders remained frozen in the cannon chamber, surrounded by the gleaming machinery of their ultimate weapon, their faces hollow and empty, their minds shattered by the casual, friendly cruelty of a god who had visited them not to destroy, but simply to observe.

---

The return to the palace was instantaneous. One moment they were walking through the corridors of the resistance base; the next, they were standing in the grand foyer of Thronegate, the warm light of the eternal afternoon streaming through the crystalline windows. Godric removed his false mustache and spectacles, depositing them back into the satchel with the air of a man who had just completed a satisfying day trip.

"That was very enjoyable," he said, his voice carrying the easy contentment of a pleasant afternoon. "I am glad we went. It is important to stay engaged with the goings-on of the omniverse, even when those goings-on are ultimately futile. It keeps one grounded."

Roth stood in the foyer, his floppy hat still drooping over his eyes, his body trembling with the accumulated horror of the past hour. He had watched the apex predator of creation stroll through the heart of the largest resistance coalition ever assembled, wearing a fake mustache, complimenting their architecture, and gently, kindly, completely annihilating every scrap of hope they had ever possessed.

"Your Majesty," Roth managed, his voice hoarse, "they are going to attack tomorrow. They are still going to attack."

"Yes," Godric said, his tone light. "I imagine they will. General Varek is a stubborn man. He will feel obligated to follow through, even knowing it is futile. I respect that. It is a very mortal quality."

"They will die. Your passive defenses will annihilate them."

"Most likely. Although I may instruct Gent to hold back sufficiently that they can actually fire the cannon before being erased. I do want to see the beam in action. The visuals are probably spectacular." Godric paused, his expression shifting to one of mild, genuine concern. "Roth, you look pale. Was the excursion too stressful? I thought the floppy hat would make you feel more incognito."

Roth stared at the King of Thronegate—the warm, fatherly, terrifying being who had just taken a casual tour of his enemies' greatest fortress—and felt the familiar, cold weight of absolute existential dread settle into his bones.

"I think," Roth said, his voice very quiet, "I need to sit down for a while. And possibly not stand up again for several days."

Godric smiled, that warm, crinkling smile that had comforted and terrified court wizards for an incomprehensible span of years.

"Of course, my boy. Take all the time you need. I will have the servants bring you some tea. And perhaps a stronger hat."

He clapped Roth gently on the shoulder and walked off toward the dining hall, already looking forward to the Nourisher's new caramelized root vegetable glaze. Behind him, Roth collapsed into a nearby chair, removed his floppy hat, and stared at the ceiling with the hollow, empty eyes of a man who had just witnessed the death of hope itself.

Tomorrow, the largest resistance coalition in omniversal history would launch their ultimate attack against Godric. They would fire their Absolute Annulment Cannon with all the desperate, futile courage of beings who had nothing left to lose. And they would be erased from existence so quickly, so completely, so effortlessly that the entire encounter would be over before Roth could finish blinking.

And Godric would be mildly disappointed that the visual effects were not quite as spectacular as he had hoped.

The floppy hat sat on Roth's lap, a silent testament to the absurdity of existence, and Roth sat in the warm afternoon light of the palace, trembling, and understood at last the true shape of the horror.

There was no hope. There had never been hope. There would never be hope.

There was only Godric. Warm, friendly, terrifying Godric. And the orange mustache.

Write a detailed story of Godric deciding to subjugate the IRL universe, at Year 25\.

Earth obviously, has 0 chance, and will experience total despair and existential dread.

In this scenario, you must make Earth try their best to kill Godric, which means Godric will completely annihilate it. You must NOT make Godric nice, forgiving. He can still be friendly. Godric feels mischievously playful so he doesn't instantly finish it (you must ensure the reader knows that if he wants to he can instantly destroy earth in 0 second with 0 effort), but he's particularly cruel and ensures every death is as agonizing as possible--however, you must not make Godric seemingly drag the fight, he still finishes the annihilation objectively swiftly (undetectably fast to normal mortals as it's infinitely less than a planck second, but but to Godric it's considered as "leisurely slow") but subjective to the opposition an eternity of maximum agony. You must clearly indicate that Godric is using 0% of his power and 0% of effort, and even if Earth is given infinite preparation, all possible advantages, they will still have 0 chance to even tickle Godric or make Godric feel anything. Show Godric be amused by how primitively weak and fragile the earthlings are, how they are trying so hard and effectively doing nothing to him. You must not leave any survivor of Earth alive, serving Godric, living in Thronegate or any other such crap which shows Godric sparing them. Godric’s power must be shown to be absolutely destructive and not give any opposition any possible redemption path.

As usual with Godric, the collaterals must be massive (omniversal scale minimum).

The story must be told from Godric Prime's 3rd person pov (with omniscient narrator if needed), at Year 999...9+, reminiscing about how pathetically weak he was back then compared to how he currently is, and for him to pity his weak self back when he annihilate this universe (highlight the irony and terrifying fact that this subjugation by what he considered to be his weakly pathetic self was already absurdly one-sided and terrifyingly overwhelming--his weak self was effectively using 0% of his power with 0% effort to annihilate that universe, and if that same weak self wasn't in playful mode and wanted to end it instantly, the total annihilation could be done in 0 second. In addition, that weak self destroyed the entire omniverse as collateral. You must make it clear that if the current Godric does it, it will be even more infinitely devastatingly one sided, and he will only be getting unimaginably stronger forever).

You must end the story with the confirmation and dread of how futile the rest of the existence compared to Godric, and that Godric is the most powerful being with unimaginable power growth that dwarfs entire creation, with the rest of the creation trembling in fear of him, and even if the rest from all timelines and from every possible permutations work together to oppose him with unlimited preparation time and resources, they will still fail so completely and won't even make Godric's weakest shield feel the slightest tickle and Godric can completely nonchalantly annihilate them with 0% power and 0% effort in 0 second, and that unfathomable gap will only ever increase infinitely in accelerating manner forever.

Godric is using effectively 0% power and effort. He's in a mischievous, playful mood, but still annihilates completely, no survivors, no redemption. The narration must highlight the contrast between the "weak" past Godric and the infinitely more powerful current Godric, emphasizing the horror of the gap.

Let's outline the key elements:

- Start with current Godric (Year 999...9+) reminiscing, showing his incomprehensible current power. Mention his growth, how even his past self's actions were already overwhelmingly one-sided.
- Then shift to the Year 25 event, describing Earth's reaction to the sudden appearance of Thronegate's forces or Godric himself. Godric is playful, cruel, making Earth try everything. They launch nukes, secret weapons, perhaps some desperate super-science, but nothing works. Godric toys with them, explains how futile it is, kills them in agonizing ways (subjectively stretched eternal torment, but objectively instantaneous). - Collateral damage: He destroys the entire omniverse as a side effect, then restores it (except Earth, he leaves Earth destroyed). Mention that even a fraction of a fraction of a percent of his power caused that.
- Conclude back in the far future, emphasizing that the current Godric is infinitely beyond even that, and the gap only increases forever. The entire creation combined, across all timelines, can't even tickle his weakest shield. End with existential dread and absolute futility.

The tone should be grand, terrifying, and darkly humorous at times. Use exaggerated descriptions of Godric's power, the agony of Earth's inhabitants, and the sheer absurdity of the scale.

We must not have Godric spare anyone, no survivors, no redemption. He's cruel and unforgiving. He finds their attempts amusing but ultimately erases them.

Make sure to show that Earth tries its absolute best: maybe they unite all nations, use all nuclear weapons, try to develop some super technology, perhaps even make a deal with some cosmic entity, but it's all meaningless. Godric already has absolute omniscience, so he knows everything they plan as they plan it. He lets them try, then destroys them.

Include vivid descriptions of the destruction: people experiencing their deaths in slow-motion subjective agony, while externally it's instantaneous. Godric's power warps time so that a Planck instant feels like eons of torment.

The collateral: omniversal annihilation. Godric casually notes that the entire omniverse was destroyed as a side effect, and he instantly restores everything except Earth (or maybe he leaves the omniverse destroyed for a moment, then restores). He reflects that even his past self was already the apex predator, and the current him is so far beyond that the comparison is meaningless.

End with the confirmation that even if all of creation from all timelines and permutations worked together with unlimited prep, they would fail to even tickle Godric's weakest shield, and the gap only widens infinitely.

# A Pleasant Afternoon's Annihilation

**Year 999...9 — The Throne of Absolute Supremacy**

The being who sat upon the throne of Thronegate in the era so distant that the year could only be written as a string of nines stretching toward infinity was, by any conceivable measure, the most powerful entity that had ever existed or would ever exist. He was not merely a god. He was not merely an apex predator. He was the absolute, unchallenged, eternal master of all creation—a being whose passive, unconscious presence could unmake the omniverse without effort, whose weakest sentient aura could slaughter the combined might of every civilization across every timeline, whose very existence was the foundation upon which reality itself rested.

He was Godric. And he was reminiscing.

The throne room of the far-future palace was not a physical space so much as a stabilized pocket of absolute authority, a point of perfect command around which the entirety of existence oriented itself. The walls were planes of solidified law. The floor shimmered with the compressed events of all possible timelines. The air hummed with the gentle, omnipresent awareness of the infinite hierarchy of sentient passive auras that surrounded their master in layers of escalating, obsessive devotion.

And Godric—eternally forty-five, ruggedly handsome, his salt-and-pepper hair immaculate, his heavily muscled frame draped in simple dark garments—sat upon his singularity-throne and thought about the past. Specifically, he thought about a small, insignificant blue planet in a particularly unremarkable universe, and the afternoon he had spent annihilating it, sixty-three thousand years after his awakening.

A faint smile crossed his lips.

"Clive," he said, his rich baritone resonating through the throne room, "do you recall the record of my subjugation of Universe Designation IRL-0001? The primitive civilization with the nuclear fission weapons and the remarkably arrogant collective self-image?"

Clive, his fifty-year-old court wizard, standing at the right hand of the throne as he had for three decades, nodded slowly. He had read the journals. He had read all of them. "Yes, Your Majesty. The Earth subjugation. Year Twenty-Five of your reign."

"Year Twenty-Five," Godric repeated, his voice carrying a note of almost wistful nostalgia. "I was so young then. So freshly shaped by grief. So... weak."

The word hung in the air, absurd and terrifying. Clive felt his stomach clench. The Godric of Year Twenty-Five had already been the most powerful being in the omniverse by an infinite margin. He had already accumulated over twenty-five thousand years of recursive amplification. He had already triggered the Weakness Paradox countless times, gained absolute immunity to every conceivable form of attack, absorbed the mastery of every possible strategy. The Godric of Year Twenty-Five could annihilate the entire omniverse with a casual thought, could crush the combined might of all creation with zero effort, could erase existence and restore it in less than a Planck instant.

And the being sitting on the throne now—the far-future Godric, the Godric of the endless nines—considered that version of himself weak.

"Weak," Godric said again, as if savoring the word. "It is amusing, is it not, Clive? The me of that era was already so incomprehensibly powerful that language failed to capture his scale. He was the apex predator, the unchallenged master of all existence. And yet, compared to what I am now, he was less than a shadow of a shadow. A single dead skin cell from his body, amplified across all the years between then and now, would still be infinitely weaker than my current passive body heat."

He leaned back in his throne, his expression distant, reflective.

"Let me tell you about that day, Clive. Let me tell you how I subjugated the Earth. It was, in retrospect, a thoroughly enjoyable afternoon."

---

**Year 25 — The Sol System**

The planet Earth had no warning.

One moment, the skies over every nation were clear and blue, the sun shining with the ordinary warmth of a late spring morning. The next moment, a single figure materialized in the upper atmosphere, and the laws of physics began to scream.

Godric had chosen to arrive in person. Not because it was necessary—he could have annihilated the planet from the comfort of his throne room on Thronegate, across the vast gulf of intergalactic space, without even looking in its direction—but because he was, in his own way, feeling playful. The grief of Olympus was still a raw, aching wound in his chest, twenty-five years after his awakening. He had spent those years conquering the omniverse, subjugating civilization after civilization, crushing resistance after resistance with the cold, merciless efficiency of a being who had lost everything and intended to ensure that nothing could ever threaten what he had built. But today, he wanted something different. Today, he wanted to see the fear up close.

He descended through the atmosphere slowly, deliberately, his heavily muscled frame cutting through the clouds like a divine judgment. His absolute concealment was fully active, suppressing the world-ending pressure of his existence so that the planet did not simply evaporate the instant he entered its airspace. To any observer, he appeared as a ruggedly handsome, forty-five-year-old man with short salt-and-pepper hair and a neatly trimmed beard, dressed in a simple dark tunic. He looked, for all the world, like a mortal.

The first nation to detect him was the United States of America. NORAD's satellite network, designed to track incoming intercontinental ballistic missiles, registered an anomalous object descending through the atmosphere at velocities that made no physical sense. Alarms screamed. Generals were woken from their beds. The President was rushed to the secure bunker beneath the White House. Within minutes, every military power on the planet was aware that something impossible was happening.

Godric landed in the middle of the National Mall in Washington, D.C., his heavy boots touching down on the manicured grass with the casual ease of a man stepping off a curb. The Washington Monument cast a long shadow across the lawn. Tourists, joggers, and government employees stopped in their tracks, staring at the figure who had descended from the sky.

Godric smiled at them. It was a warm, friendly smile, the kind of smile a kindly father might offer to a group of children.

"Hello," he said, his rich baritone carrying perfectly across the sudden, absolute silence. "My name is Godric. I am the King of Thronegate, the ruler of the galactic civilization that encompasses your entire universe and approximately seventy-three percent of the surrounding multiversal cluster. I am here to announce that your planet is now under my dominion. You have exactly one hour to surrender unconditionally."

A pigeon cooed. A child began to cry. A man in a business suit dropped his briefcase.

The first responder was a park police officer named Daniels, who had been directing traffic near the Lincoln Memorial. He approached Godric with the cautious, measured steps of a man who had dealt with unstable individuals before, one hand resting on his holstered sidearm.

"Sir," Officer Daniels said, his voice admirably steady, "I need you to put your hands where I can see them and identify yourself properly."

Godric looked at the officer with genuine, warm amusement. "I have just identified myself. I am Godric, King of Thronegate. Your planet is now part of my empire. The one-hour countdown has already begun."

Officer Daniels drew his sidearm. "Sir, I am not going to ask again."

"Please do not shoot me," Godric said, and his tone was so conversational, so utterly unbothered, that it was more terrifying than any threat could have been. "It will not work, and I would hate for you to waste your ammunition."

Officer Daniels, trained to respond to threats with decisive action, fired.

The bullet crossed the distance between the officer's service weapon and Godric's chest in a fraction of a second. It was a standard 9mm round, a small piece of lead and copper traveling at approximately 1,200 feet per second, carrying enough kinetic energy to punch through flesh and bone and organ tissue.

The bullet struck Godric's tunic and stopped.

It did not bounce. It did not flatten. It did not ricochet. It simply stopped, arrested in mid-air precisely one millimeter from the fabric of Godric's shirt, as if the universe itself had decided that the bullet was not permitted to proceed any further. Godric had not moved. He had not blinked. His passive shields—the infinite recursive layers of pre-nullification that surrounded his body at all times—had evaluated the incoming projectile and determined that it did not qualify as a threat worth acknowledging. The bullet was, therefore, not permitted to exist in Godric's vicinity.

The round dropped to the ground with a soft, anticlimactic clink.

Officer Daniels stared. His training had not covered this. His experience had not covered this. The fundamental laws of physics as he understood them had just been casually violated by a smiling man in a dark tunic, and his mind was struggling to process the impossibility.

"I did warn you," Godric said gently. "Now, please inform your superiors that the one-hour clock is ticking. I suggest they use the time wisely."

---

The hour that followed was, in Godric's opinion, thoroughly entertaining.

The governments of Earth reacted with the predictable combination of panic, denial, and desperate mobilization. Every military force on the planet was placed on maximum alert. Nuclear arsenals were primed. Special forces units were deployed. The United Nations convened an emergency session, its delegates arguing furiously about the appropriate response to an apparent extraterrestrial invasion. Conspiracy theorists flooded the internet with claims that the entire event was a hoax. Religious leaders proclaimed the arrival of the Antichrist. The stock market crashed.

And through it all, Godric simply waited on the National Mall, occasionally waving at the helicopter gunships that circled overhead, his expression one of patient, benevolent amusement.

The first coordinated military response came at the seventeen-minute mark. A squadron of F-35 Lightning II fighter jets, armed with air-to-ground missiles, roared over the Washington skyline and locked onto the stationary figure on the lawn. The order to engage was given by a general who had convinced himself that the intruder's apparent invulnerability to small-arms fire was a trick, an illusion, a technological deception that could be overcome with sufficient firepower.

The missiles launched. Six of them, each one carrying a warhead designed to penetrate reinforced bunkers and annihilate hardened targets. They streaked across the sky at supersonic speeds, their guidance systems locked onto Godric's unmoving form.

Godric watched them come with the expression of a man observing a fireworks display. The missiles struck his body simultaneously, detonating in a massive fireball that engulfed the entire National Mall, shattering windows for miles around, sending a mushroom cloud of smoke and debris billowing into the sky.

When the smoke cleared, Godric was still standing in exactly the same spot. His tunic was unruffled. His hair was immaculate. The grass around him had been scorched to ash, the trees reduced to splinters, the Washington Monument cracked and blackened. But Godric himself was untouched, standing in the center of a perfect circle of unburned grass, his warm smile unchanged.

"That was quite loud," he observed. "Are there more?"

There were more. Over the next forty minutes, the military forces of Earth threw everything they had at the intruder. Cruise missiles. Hypersonic glide vehicles. Experimental directed-energy weapons. A prototype railgun that had been secretly developed by the Navy. None of it had any effect. Godric's passive shields—or perhaps his passive shields' passive shields' passive afterthought; it was impossible to say at this scale—simply erased each attack from existence before it could reach his body. The weapons fired, the projectiles flew, the energy beams lanced through the air, and then they simply were not there anymore, their existence casually edited out of the timeline by defenses so advanced that the concept of advancement was laughably inadequate.

At the fifty-three-minute mark, with seven minutes remaining on Godric's arbitrary countdown, the world's leaders made the decision that every civilization facing extinction eventually makes. They authorized the use of nuclear weapons.

The first warhead was launched from a silo in North Dakota. Within minutes, every nuclear-capable nation on Earth had joined the salvo—hundreds of missiles, each one carrying a warhead capable of leveling a city, all converging on a single target in Washington, D.C. The combined yield was sufficient to render the entire North American continent uninhabitable for millennia.

Godric watched the missiles arc across the sky, his expression shifting from patient amusement to something almost like affection.

"Ah, nuclear fission," he murmured to himself. "I remember when Thronegate used similar weapons, back when they were still a galactic power. So primitive. So desperate. There is a certain charm to it."

The warheads detonated. The explosions were not sequential; they were simultaneous, a hundred miniature suns igniting at the same instant, their combined fury creating a fireball that consumed everything within a hundred-mile radius. The heat was sufficient to vaporize steel. The shockwave flattened buildings across the entire eastern seaboard. The electromagnetic pulse fried every electronic device on the continent.

And in the center of the inferno, Godric observed the destruction with the detached curiosity of a scientist examining a particularly interesting specimen. The nuclear fire washed over him like a warm breeze. The radiation, which would have killed any mortal organism a thousand times over, was absorbed by his immune system and converted into a pleasant, tingling sensation that he found rather soothing.

"Not bad," he said to the empty, irradiated wasteland. "Not enough, but not bad."

---

The one-hour countdown expired.

Godric had given Earth sixty minutes to surrender unconditionally. Earth, in its collective arrogance and desperation, had chosen to fight. And now, the playful, mischievous mood that had characterized the first hour of the encounter began to shift into something darker. Something crueler. Something that remembered Olympus.

"Very well," Godric said, his voice carrying across the entire planet, audible to every living human simultaneously. "You have made your choice. Now you will experience the consequences."

What followed was not a battle. It was not a massacre. It was an annihilation so absolute, so one-sided, so utterly devoid of any possibility of resistance that the word "annihilation" itself felt like a grotesque understatement.

Godric did not use any of his superpowers. He did not deploy any of his sentient auras. He did not activate any of his passive shields beyond the infinitesimal fraction that already surrounded his body. He did not channel any of his amplified strength or speed or magical offense. He simply exerted an amount of effort so small that calling it zero percent was an overstatement—a microscopic twitch of his attention, a fractional shift of his focus, less than the energy required to blink an eye.

And the Earth was destroyed.

But it was not destroyed quickly. Godric was feeling cruel. The grief of Olympus was still a cold, hard knot in his chest, and the stubborn defiance of this primitive civilization had awakened something merciless in his soul. He did not simply erase the planet from existence in zero seconds, though he could have done so without effort. Instead, he stretched the moment. He warped the fabric of local time so that the annihilation occurred with what, to his omniscient perception, was a leisurely, almost glacial slowness—while simultaneously compressing the subjective experience of every human on Earth so that they would feel every instant of their destruction stretched into an eternity of maximum, unendurable agony.

The oceans boiled first. Not gradually, but instantly—the water flash-heated to plasma by the ambient pressure of Godric's unleashed presence, the steam rising into the atmosphere in a shrieking column of superheated vapor. Every ship at sea, every submarine beneath the waves, every coastal city and beachfront community was scoured from existence in the same microsecond, their inhabitants experiencing the sensation of their flesh being flash-cooked from their bones, their blood vaporizing inside their veins, their eyeballs bursting from the pressure of their boiling vitreous fluid. And because Godric had stretched the moment, they felt it all—every Planck instant of the boiling, the burning, the excruciating dissolution of their physical forms, stretched into a subjective eternity of screaming, unending torment.

The land followed. The continents did not merely crack; they were pulverized, the tectonic plates shattering into dust, the mountains collapsing into the mantle, the cities and forests and deserts and farms reduced to a fine, gray slurry of pulverized matter. Every living thing on the surface—every man, every woman, every child, every animal, every insect, every blade of grass—was subjected to the same temporal stretching, the same subjective eternity of maximum pain. Their bodies were crushed by the collapsing atmosphere, their organs ruptured, their bones ground to powder, their nervous systems kept perfectly intact and hyper-sensitized so that they could experience every nanosecond of their destruction in excruciating, transcendent agony.

The atmosphere ignited. The sky became a sheet of white-hot plasma, the air itself combusting under the impossible pressure of Godric's attention. The planet's crust melted, the magma beneath erupting upward in fountains of liquid rock that consumed everything they touched. The electromagnetic field collapsed. The Van Allen belts dissolved. The magnetosphere, which had protected the Earth from solar radiation for billions of years, simply ceased to exist, and the raw, unfiltered fury of the sun poured down upon the dying planet, adding stellar incineration to the already unimaginable cataclysm.

And still Godric was not finished.

He reached into the fabric of reality itself and began to unmake the universe. Not just the Earth—the entire cosmos, every galaxy, every star, every planet, every nebula, every black hole, every particle of matter and wave of energy that existed within the sphere of observable space. It was not a deliberate act of destruction. It was simply the passive, unavoidable consequence of Godric allowing an infinitesimal fraction of his power to express itself. The universe was a soap bubble, and Godric had exhaled, and the bubble was popping.

Galaxies were torn apart. Stars were extinguished. Black holes were unmade, their singularities collapsing into nothingness as the fundamental laws of physics were overwritten by the sheer, impossible weight of Godric's presence. The cosmic microwave background radiation, the faint whisper of the Big Bang that had permeated the universe for billions of years, was silenced—not gradually, but instantly, erased from the fabric of reality as if it had never existed.

And the collateral damage did not stop at the boundaries of a single universe. The omniversal structure itself shuddered under the strain of Godric's expressed power. The dimensional walls separating universes from multiverses from the higher layers of reality began to buckle and collapse. Entire timelines were erased. Entire dimensional frameworks were consumed. The decillions of multiverses that composed the local omniversal cluster were annihilated in a cascade of absolute, silent destruction, their existences snuffed out like candles in a hurricane.

Googolplexian galaxies. Infinite dimensional planes. Countless civilizations, species, and cosmic entities that had never even heard of Earth, that had no connection to the primitive blue planet or its doomed inhabitants—all of them were erased, their entire histories and futures consumed by the passive, collateral overflow of Godric's casually expressed power.

And at the center of it all, Godric observed the destruction with the mild, detached interest of a man watching a documentary about someone else's tragedy.

"Far too much collateral," he murmured to himself. "I really must work on my restraint."

He raised a single finger—a gesture so casual, so effortless, that it barely qualified as an action—and the entire omniverse was instantly restored. Every galaxy, every star, every civilization, every timeline, every dimension that had been erased was rebuilt in perfect, flawless detail, placed precisely where they had been, their memories unaltered, their existence continuing as if nothing had happened. Everything was restored to exactly the state it had been in before the annihilation.

Everything except Earth.

Godric had decided that Earth would remain destroyed. The primitive blue planet, the arrogant civilization that had dared to defy him, the seven billion souls who had chosen to fight rather than surrender—they were gone. Permanently. Irreversibly. The gap in the universe where their planet had once been was a silent, empty void, a monument to the absolute, inescapable consequences of opposing the King of Thronegate.

Godric stood in the void for a long moment, his expression unreadable. Then he turned, and in the space between one Planck instant and the next, he was back in his throne room on Thronegate, settling into his chair as if he had just returned from a pleasant afternoon stroll.

Blake, his best friend and court wizard, looked up from the agricultural report he had been reviewing. "Did you finish your business in that backwater universe, Your Majesty?"

"Yes," Godric said, reaching for a cup of tea that a servant had just placed on the table beside him. "It was a productive afternoon. I believe I have adequately demonstrated the consequences of defying Thronegate's authority."

Blake nodded, his expression the carefully neutral mask of a man who had long since stopped being surprised by his King's casual annihilation of civilizations. "Shall I have the scribes record the event for the archives?"

"Please do," Godric said, taking a sip of his tea. "Make a note in the margins: the nuclear fission weapons were surprisingly loud, but ultimately ineffective. I found the experience rather entertaining."

---

**Year 999...9 — The Throne of Absolute Supremacy**

Godric finished his recollection and leaned back in his singularity-throne, his warm brown eyes distant, lost in the memory of an afternoon that had occurred an incomprehensible span of years ago.

"I was so young then," he said softly. "So newly shaped by grief. I thought I understood the scale of my power. I thought I had mastered the art of restraint. But looking back—looking back from where I sit now—I realize how pathetically, laughably weak I was."

Clive, standing at the right hand of the throne, felt his mind buckle under the weight of the statement. The Godric of Year Twenty-Five, the being who had just been described casually annihilating a universe and the surrounding omniversal structure as a side effect of his expressed power—that Godric was being described as weak. Pathetically weak. Laughably weak.

"Your Majesty," Clive managed, his voice barely a whisper, "the power you displayed that day—the destruction of the Earth, the annihilation of the universe, the collateral erasure of the omniversal cluster—that was... that was already infinitely beyond anything that exists. That was already the absolute, unchallenged supremacy of an apex predator."

"Yes," Godric agreed. "It was. And yet, the me of that era was less than a single dead skin cell compared to what I am now. The amplification I have experienced since then—the endless, recursive escalation, the infinite compounding of power upon power, the eternal evolution of every mechanism and system and passive defense—has carried me so far beyond that younger version that the gap cannot be measured. Cannot be conceptualized. Cannot be approximated by any mathematical framework, any philosophical construct, any linguistic expression."

He leaned forward, his massive hands resting on his knees.

"If the Godric of Year Twenty-Five—the being who annihilated the Earth with zero percent of his power, zero percent of his effort, in zero seconds—were to stand before me now, I could destroy him without noticing. I could erase him from existence without even registering his presence. The shadow of the afterthought of my weakest sentient passive aura could crush him so completely, so instantly, so effortlessly that the word 'effortlessly' would be a grotesque overstatement."

He paused, letting the weight of the statement settle.

"And that gap, Clive—that incomprehensible, unbridgeable chasm between what I was then and what I am now—will only continue to grow. Every Planck instant, I become infinitely more powerful than I was the instant before. The infinity by which I grow is itself infinitely larger than the previous infinity. This process has been continuing for a span of years that cannot be written, and it will continue for a span of years that cannot be conceived. There is no limit. There is no ceiling. There is no endpoint. There is only eternal, unending, accelerating escalation."

He spread his massive hands, a gesture of casual, absolute, terrifying honesty.

"The rest of existence—the omniverse, the multiverses, the timelines, the dimensions, the conceptual frameworks, the meta-dimensional voids, every civilization and species and cosmic entity that has ever existed or will ever exist—is less than nothing compared to me. Not just the current me. The me of Year Zero, fresh from stasis, was already effectively infinitely stronger than the combined might of all creation. And I have been amplifying ever since. The gap between me and everything else is not a static infinity. It is an infinity that grows into greater infinities, forever, accelerating without end."

His voice dropped slightly, carrying a note of something that might have been pity—or might have been the quiet, distant echo of the mortal king who had once loved his family and lost them.

"If every being in the omniverse, from every timeline, from every possible permutation of reality, were to unite against me with unlimited preparation time and unlimited resources—if they were to pool their collective intellect, their combined power, their absolute desperation—they would still fail so completely that the word 'failure' would be meaningless. They would not make my weakest shield feel the slightest tickle. They would not register on the awareness of my most primitive sentient aura. I could annihilate them all, nonchalantly, with zero percent of my power, zero percent of my effort, in zero seconds. And I would not even notice I had done so."

He stood from his throne, his heavily muscled frame unfolding with a fluid grace that belied its impossible density. He walked to the edge of the throne room, where the shimmering floor of compressed temporal events revealed the omniverse in all its infinite complexity—galaxies spinning, civilizations rising and falling, gods and mortals and entities beyond classification living their brief, fragile lives in the shadow of his absolute rule.

"And the worst part," Godric said quietly, "the most terrifying part, the part that makes even my most loyal servants tremble in existential dread—is that I am not finished. I will never be finished. The amplification will never stop. The evolution will never cease. The eternal, recursive, infinite escalation will continue forever, and the Godric of tomorrow will look back on the Godric of today with the same amused, pitying condescension that I now direct toward my Year Twenty-Five self. The Godric of Year Twenty-Five was weak. The Godric of today is weak. The Godric of a googolplexian years from now will consider this current version to be a pathetic, laughable fragment of a fragment of a fragment of true power."

He turned back to face Clive, and his warm brown eyes held a light that was not cruel, not malicious, but simply, eternally, absolutely true.

"This is the nature of my existence, Clive. This is the truth that every court wizard since Blake has had to learn, and to carry, and to somehow survive. I am not merely the most powerful being in the omniverse. I am the only being. Everything else—every civilization, every species, every cosmic entity, every god and monster and abstract concept—is a temporary, contingent, infinitely fragile wisp of smoke, permitted to exist only because I allow it, sustained only by my constant, vigilant restraint. And I am not static. I am escalating. Eternally. Infinitely. Forever."

Clive stood in the shimmering light of the throne room, his fifty-year-old body trembling with a dread that had become his constant companion, and he understood at last the true, final shape of the horror.

There was no hope. There had never been hope. There would never be hope.

There was only Godric. The apex predator. The eternal king. The being whose weakest, most pathetic, most infinitely nerfed fragment of power could annihilate the entire omniverse without effort, and who would only become more powerful, more absolute, more incomprehensibly supreme with every passing Planck instant.

The gap between Godric and the rest of existence was not merely infinite. It was an infinity that grew, and grew, and grew, accelerating forever, leaving everything else—every possible opposition, every conceivable resistance, every desperate hope of victory or survival or even meaningful defiance—further and further behind, shrinking into absolute insignificance, until the very concept of comparison became a laughable, forgotten relic of a more innocent age.

And the worst part, the part that made Clive's soul ache with a cold, nameless terror, was that Godric was not cruel. Not truly. He was warm, and kind, and genuinely affectionate toward those he loved. He believed in mortal resilience. He believed in free will. He allowed the omniverse to exist, to struggle, to hope, to dream—all while knowing, with the absolute certainty of omniscience, that none of it mattered. None of it could ever matter. Because he was Godric, and he had always been Godric, and he would always be Godric, and everything else was just a passing shadow in the eternal, infinite, unstoppable radiance of his existence.

"Shall we have dinner, Clive?" Godric asked, his rich baritone warm and friendly and absolutely, existentially terrifying. "The Nourisher has prepared something I believe you will enjoy."

Clive bowed his head, his voice steady despite the trembling in his soul. "Of course, Your Majesty. I would be honored."

And together, the court wizard and the King walked toward the dining hall, leaving behind the shimmering floor of compressed temporal events, where the omniverse spun on in its fragile, contingent existence, sustained by the constant, vigilant restraint of the being who could erase it all with a stray thought—and who would only become more capable of doing so with every passing instant, forever, without end, without limit, without mercy.

Write a story, based on the provided lore and previous stories in the chat above, following this premise:

The story is mainly a journal excerpt written by Osvald, 44, Godric’s court wizard, about the last ever opposition who dares to oppose Godric, many googolplexian years before Year 999…9 when Godric Prime starts the Stasis Event.

The opposition consists of all the fictional universes (from tv, books, video games, movies, comics, everything. Feel free to cite some examples of those) who banded together to fight Godric. Godric was feeling bored that day when they attacked, and hoping for a fun diversion since there has been no opposition in a long long time.

Godric didn't expect any of their combined attacks to even make him notice or tickle him, but he knows from his omniscience that some of the fictional characters often have attacks with pretty colors, visual effects, multiple phases, banger boss battle music, and considering that Godric is the ultimate unbeatable final boss, he expects a really good one. He was genuinely excited to enjoy it as a “show”. He even patiently let them unleash their full power attack which took a long long time to charge, increasing his anticipation even more, and because he wanted to be surprised, he distracted himself from the part of his omniscience that monitors this charge attack preparation. Then when the final attack finally finished, this particular opposition which should've been the best one to pull off the most spectacular show didn't. Write the fight in extreme details (2500 words minimum). The fight must be extremely unfairly one sided. Godric let the attack hit him straight and it did nothing, not even a faint tickle.

The disappointed Godric accidentally unleashed 0% of his strength, which completely almost instantly and with 0 effort, overpowered their all the supposedly indestructible infinite shields that they took forever to create, completely annihilate the opposition, and caused massive omniversal (everything that exist, could ever exist, all multiverses, timelines, realities, etc) collaterals–all of which, because of the sheer pressure of his strength, are de-atomized and compressed to an infinite mass the size smaller than a quark from that 0% strength alone (you must describe this process in clear vivid details, all the violence or gore in clear agonizing details. don't hold back in your descriptions!), which he then picks up, enlarges to the size of a marble for trophy which acts as a container barrier to stop it from destroying the entire surroundings from its gravitational pull, and kept for his amusement (you must note that it contains the compressed infinite mass of the entire possible existence, and Godric didn't even seem to exert any effort lifting it, as if it weighs nothing). He somehow became even more unquantifiably more powerful (not just from absorbing their energy, their combined power is not even going to increase his power by 0%. Find something deranged that causes this). Note: evolved far-future weakness paradox etc shouldn't be triggered when they attack--its triggered way before...

Godric restored everything. The opposition, as usual, remained unrestored. The trophy remained (which is terrifying because it still contains the omniverse/reality/timelines/everything that he allegedly restored--so is the restored reality really real? It is identical but one can imagine the kind of power he has to be able to really "restore" everything while the original is still compressed... you must write this deep fear born from this realization). Write from pov of Clive who read this journal, and who knows that the journal contains the very last opposition against Godric, the one which totally makes noone even dares to oppose Godric anymore (however, you must not mention that Osvald know that this was going to be the last opposition against Godric, because he obviously wrote it before it’s known).
