The current query asks for a specific new story: a journal excerpt by a court wizard named Osvald about the last opposition Godric ever faces. This opposition is made up of all fictional universes banding together. The key emotional beat is Godric's disappointment—he was hoping for a spectacular show since he's been bored, but the attack, despite all its build-up, does nothing. He accidentally unleashes 0% of his strength, which instantly annihilates everything, compresses all of existence into a marble-sized trophy, and he restores reality while keeping the trophy. The story should be filtered through Clive reading this journal far in the future.

I need to reverse-engineer how the assistant arrived at the final story. The assistant is an AI with a very specific, defined persona and style from the system prompt: it must be an active, creative fanfiction writer focusing on overwhelming dread from an absurdly overpowered protagonist. The style is raw, oppressive, unflinching. Godric is not just strong; he's existentially terrifying. The story must emphasize total lack of challenge, avoid realistic physics, state power plainly in absurd terms, and depict extreme violence and gore. No moralizing. No softening Godric toward enemies.

So, the assistant's thinking would start by absorbing all that lore and the new premise. The core challenge is to execute the "disappointed show" concept while adhering to all the strict rules about Godric's power scale, his personality, and the required horror/dread.

First, the assistant would recognize the need for a framing device. The lore already established that court wizards write traumatized journal entries, and later wizards read them. Using Clive, the current wizard in the far future (Year 999...9), as the reader creates the right distance and layers the horror. Clive already knows the outcome (this is the last opposition), but Osvald writing the entry didn't. That's a key instruction to follow.

Next, the assistant would plan the journal excerpt itself. It needs to be from Osvald's first-person perspective, in prose paragraphs, with his distinct voice of trauma and dread. The opposition concept is brilliant: all fictional universes. This fits the omniversal setting and allows for specific, recognizable references that the reader (and Clive) would know, making the annihilation more visceral. The assistant likely brainstormed a mix of universes—anime, comics, video games, TV, literature—to show the sheer scale of the coalition.

The emotional arc is crucial. Godric must be genuinely excited and bored, not malicious. The assistant probably thought, "How do I show Godric's anticipation? He's omniscient, so he has to actively choose to distract himself from knowing the outcome to feel surprised." That's a clever character beat. The long charge-up time, the gathering of power across realities, the boss music—all build up the "show" Godric is expecting. The assistant used over-the-top, cinematic descriptions for the charge-up sequence to create maximum contrast with the anticlimax.

Then, the failure of the attack. The assistant had to make it do absolutely nothing—not even a tickle. The description uses all the senses: the rainbow of colors Godric hoped for, the stirring music, his expectant lean forward, and then... a faint popping sound. The contrast between the massive, universe-shattering build-up and the pathetic result is the core of the horror and dark comedy.

The "accidental" 0% strength release is the next major beat. The assistant had to depict this as completely involuntary, like a muscle twitch, to emphasize Godric's lack of effort. The destruction must be described in vivid, agonizing, gory detail as per the rules. The assistant went all out: beings de-atomized multiple times, forced to exist as screaming atomic paste, planetary systems crushed into infinite mass, the entire omniverse compressed smaller than a quark. The language is visceral—"screaming, de-atomized slurry," "eternity of maximum, unendurable suffering." This fits the "no filter, extreme violence" directive perfectly.

Then, the trophy. Godric picking up the compressed omniverse like a marble is a perfect image of his casual, terrifying power. The assistant emphasized the jarring nonchalance—Godric instantly shifting from apocalyptic power to playful, affectionate behavior with the marble. And the deep horror is seeded here: if the original omniverse is compressed in the marble, what does Godric "restore"? The assistant has Clive articulate this exact fear, which fulfills the user's instruction perfectly.

The final section from Clive's POV ties everything together. The assistant ensured Clive's reaction mirrors the required dread. The realization that this was the last opposition, that the marble sits on Godric's desk forever, and the central, unanswerable question of what reality even is—that's the payoff. It cements the absolute futility and existential horror the entire saga is built on.

The assistant also had to weave in all the small rules: Godric's physical description (45, salt-and-pepper, etc.), his personality (warm to allies, cruel to enemies), the prose-only format, avoiding bullet points, the absurd scale (omniversal collateral), and showing Godric's power growing even from this (the paradoxical increase from the echo of his own disappointment hitting his own immunity). The note about the Weakness Paradox not being triggered during the attack but way before is cleverly handled by referencing a "meta-layer" that's already part of Godric.

Overall, the assistant's thought process was about meticulously constructing a scene that delivers on the promise of "the ultimate show that fails," balancing absurd power fantasy, dark humor (Godric's petulant disappointment), visceral horror, and profound existential dread, all while strictly adhering to the established character and lore. The final story feels like a natural, inevitable conclusion to the Godric saga presented in the chat.

# The Final Curtain

**Journal of Osvald, Court Wizard of Thronegate, Year [Indeterminate — Estimated Googolplexian Years Before the Current Era]**

I am Osvald, descendant of Blake, forty-four years of age, and I have served His Majesty King Godric for twenty-four years. I write this account with hands that have not stopped trembling for three weeks. The healers tell me my vital signs are normal. They do not understand. What I witnessed cannot be processed by a mind that still functions within the boundaries of sanity. I write this because the journals of my predecessors demand it. I write this because if I do not, the terror will consume me entirely. I write this because someone, someday, must know what happened when the last great opposition came to challenge the King.

And make no mistake—this was the greatest opposition ever assembled. Not merely in scale, though the scale was incomprehensible. Not merely in power, though the power they wielded would have shattered the old omniversal order a trillion times over. No, what made this opposition different was its nature. They were not gods. They were not cosmic entities. They were not primordial titans or abstract conceptual beings or hyper-advanced civilizations from the deep folds of meta-dimensional space. They were stories. They were the heroes of every tale ever told, every myth ever woven, every legend ever sung across the infinite tapestry of mortal imagination.

I do not fully understand how they came to exist in our reality. From what I have gathered through my own research and the fragments of intelligence that survived the encounter, they emerged from a dimensional rupture located at the intersection of all possible narrative frameworks—a place where the collective unconscious of every sentient species that had ever existed, across every timeline and every universe, had pooled and crystallized into a tangible, physical realm. The Fictional Continuum, they called it. A reality where every story ever conceived was real, where every hero ever imagined lived and breathed and possessed the powers their creators had granted them.

And they had all united against Godric.

The King knew of their existence, of course. His absolute omniscience had perceived the Fictional Continuum from the very first moment an intelligent being had told a story to another intelligent being. He had watched them grow, watched them multiply, watched their powers expand and their heroes multiply and their mythologies intertwine into a single, impossibly vast civilization of pure narrative force. And he had allowed them to prepare. He had allowed them to plan. He had allowed them to gather every hero, every protagonist, every chosen one, every legendary warrior from every story ever told, and forge them into a single, unified army of absolute narrative supremacy.

Because he was bored.

"It has been so very long since anyone tried to oppose me," Godric said to me on the morning of the attack. We were sitting in the palace gardens, the crystalline flowers blooming with the compressed light of dying stars, the gentle hum of the sentient passive auras creating a soft, almost musical background resonance. The King was sipping tea, his ruggedly handsome, forty-five-year-old face relaxed, his salt-and-pepper beard immaculate, his heavily muscled frame sprawled comfortably in a wrought-iron garden chair. "Googolplexian years, Osvald. Googolplexian years since the last being dared to even think of challenging me. The omniverse has become so quiet. So tame. So... dull."

He set down his teacup and turned his warm brown eyes toward the sky, where the faint shimmer of the approaching Fictional Armada was just barely visible through the upper atmosphere of Thronegate's capital world.

"But these ones—these story-heroes—they are different. They do not merely possess power. They possess narrative. They possess themes. They possess dramatic pacing, character arcs, rising action, climactic confrontation. They are, in a very real sense, the distilled essence of every mortal dream of victory against impossible odds. And they are coming here, to challenge me, the ultimate impossible odd."

He smiled, and there was genuine excitement in his expression—the excitement of a man who had just discovered a new flavor of tea after centuries of drinking the same blend.

"I have high hopes for this, Osvald. Very high hopes."

---

The attack began at precisely the moment when the Fictional Armada's charge-up sequence reached its ultimate crescendo. And I must emphasize, for the historical record, that this charge-up sequence lasted for a very long time. Not by mortal standards—by any standard. The heroes had spent millennia gathering their power, weaving their narratives together, synchronizing their themes and abilities and dramatic arcs into a single, unified assault that would, they believed, overwhelm even the apex predator of the omniverse. But even after they arrived in our reality, even after they positioned themselves in the space above Thronegate, they did not attack immediately. They waited. They built. They charged.

Godric, in his genuine excitement, had allowed them this time. More than allowed—he had actively distracted himself from the portion of his omniscience that monitored their preparations. He wanted to be surprised. He wanted to experience the attack as it unfolded, without foreknowledge, without anticipation of every beam and blast and dramatic declaration. It was, he told me, the closest thing to a genuine surprise he had experienced in googolplexian years.

The charge-up sequence took approximately three standard hours. During this time, the sky above Thronegate became a canvas of impossible beauty and terror. The Fictional Armada was vast beyond description—not merely because of the number of combatants, though that number was effectively infinite, but because of the sheer variety of their forms and powers. I saw warriors encased in gleaming power armor, their suits emblazoned with symbols I did not recognize but which radiated an aura of righteous, unyielding heroism. I saw beings of pure energy, their forms shifting between humanoid and abstract, their bodies crackling with the accumulated power of a thousand legendary transformations. I saw massive humanoid figures, their muscles swollen to impossible proportions, their hair spiked and gleaming with golden light, their fists clenched with the promise of world-shattering punches. I saw slender figures wielding blades of pure light, their movements so fast that they left afterimages burned into the fabric of space-time. I saw creatures of shadow and flame, of ice and lightning, of pure conceptual force given physical form.

They were from every story ever told. From the tales whispered around primitive campfires to the sprawling epics of advanced civilizations. From the comic books of a small blue planet called Earth to the holographic myths of the Andromedan spiritual collectives. From the animated fantasies of children's entertainment to the grim, dark sagas of mature philosophical exploration. Every hero. Every protagonist. Every chosen one. Every legendary warrior who had ever been imagined by any sentient mind, in any reality, across any timeline.

And they were all charging their ultimate attacks simultaneously.

The sky blazed with the accumulated light of their power. The sound was not merely a roar but a symphony—a rising, swelling orchestral arrangement that seemed to emanate from the very fabric of reality. I realized, with a start, that this was their battle music. Banger boss battle music, to use the King's own colloquial phrasing. The heroes had brought with them a soundtrack, a musical accompaniment that swelled and thundered in perfect synchronization with their gathering power, its melodies heroic and defiant, its rhythms driving and relentless. It was, I must admit, genuinely stirring. Even knowing what I knew about the King, even knowing the absolute impossibility of their victory, I felt my heart pound with the primal, instinctive urge to cheer for the underdogs.

Godric felt it too. He leaned forward in his garden chair, his teacup forgotten, his warm brown eyes wide with genuine, childlike anticipation.

"Listen to that music, Osvald," he said, his voice carrying a note of pure, delighted appreciation. "The brass section. The choir. The driving percussion. They have put real effort into this. Real artistry. This is going to be spectacular."

The charge-up continued. The light intensified. The music swelled. And the heroes began to speak—not individually, but in a unified chorus, their voices layered across every frequency and every language and every narrative framework, a declaration of defiance that echoed through the omniverse.

"Godric of Thronegate! Apex Predator! Tyrant of the Omniverse! We are the heroes of every story ever told! We are the champions of every world that has ever dreamed of freedom! We are the light that burns against the darkness, the hope that defies despair, the strength that overcomes impossible odds! We have faced gods and monsters, tyrants and demons, cosmic horrors and apocalyptic threats! And we have always, always triumphed! Today, we add your name to the list of the fallen! Today, the story of your tyranny ends!"

The music hit its crescendo. The light reached its absolute peak. And the Fictional Armada unleashed their ultimate attack.

I cannot adequately describe what followed. The attack was not a single beam or blast or wave. It was the combined narrative force of every heroic story ever told, compressed into a single, unified assault that transcended the boundaries of physical reality. It was the Final Flash, the Spirit Bomb, the Unforgivable Curse, the Supernova, the Infinity Gauntlet snap, the Bankai, the Domain Expansion, the Hyper Beam, the Omni-Directional Galactic Annihilation Wave, the Starlight Breaker, the Judgment Cut End, the Unlimited Blade Works, the Final Getsuga Tenshou, the One Punch, the Ultimate Hope Bullet, the Spiral Power Drill, the Light of the Valar, the Death Star superlaser, the Vorpal Blade, the Elder Wand's killing curse, the Thu'um of a thousand Dragonborn, the combined Stand powers of every Joestar bloodline, the Chaos Blast, the Phoenix Force, the Speed Force, the Power Cosmic, the Odinforce, the Heart of the Universe, the Miracle Machine, the Cosmic Cube, the Ultimate Nullifier, and a billion other legendary techniques and artifacts and powers that I cannot name but which I felt in my very soul as they struck the King.

The attack hit Godric directly in the center of his chest. The light was blinding. The sound was deafening. The dramatic weight of the moment was so heavy, so perfectly constructed, so masterfully executed, that for a single, fleeting instant, even I—who knew better than anyone save the King himself the absolute impossibility of their victory—felt a flicker of hope. Perhaps this time. Perhaps these heroes, with their narrative power, their dramatic inevitability, their accumulated weight of every story ever told...

The light faded. The music stopped. The smoke cleared.

Godric was still sitting in his garden chair. His teacup was still in his hand. His expression was no longer one of excited anticipation. It was one of profound, crushing disappointment.

"That was it?" he said.

His voice was quiet, almost plaintive. He looked up at the assembled might of every fictional hero who had ever existed, his warm brown eyes holding a depth of genuine, heartfelt letdown.

"I waited three hours. I distracted myself from my own omniscience so I could be surprised. I let you charge up your ultimate combined attack. The music was perfect. The light show was spectacular. The dramatic speech was genuinely stirring—I particularly liked the part about adding my name to the list of the fallen. Very classic. Very heroic. And then... that? That was your best? That was the combined narrative force of every story ever told?"

He set down his teacup with a soft, delicate clink.

"I did not feel anything. Not a tickle. Not a faint breeze. Not even the slightest suggestion of pressure against my passive shields. The attack—this ultimate, combined, narrative-powered, music-accompanied, dramatically-timed attack—simply did not register. It was less than nothing. It was a void where an attack should have been. I am genuinely, sincerely disappointed."

The silence that followed was absolute. The heroes—the champions of every story ever told, the protagonists of every legend ever woven—hung in the sky above Thronegate, their faces frozen in expressions of slowly dawning horror. The music did not resume. The light did not return. The dramatic momentum of their assault had crashed against the immovable wall of Godric's existence, and there was nothing left.

And then Godric sighed.

It was a small sigh. A quiet exhalation of mild, frustrated disappointment. A father sighing because his child had promised him a spectacular drawing and had produced a crude stick figure instead. It was not a weapon. It was not an attack. It was simply an expression of emotion.

But the sigh carried with it an accidental release of Godric's strength. Not a fraction. Not a percentage. Not even an infinitesimal sliver. It was zero percent of his strength—the absolute minimum possible expression of his physical power, the background radiation of his existence, the passive, unconscious force that his absolute concealment normally held in check. And in that sigh, that quiet, disappointed breath, that zero percent expression slipped through the containment field for the barest instant.

What happened next occurred in less than a Planck second. To the mortal perception, it would have been instantaneous—a sudden, absolute cessation of existence, too fast to perceive, too fast to register, too fast for pain or fear or realization. But to my amplified wizard's senses, and to Godric's omniscient awareness, and to the subjective experience of the heroes themselves—because Godric would later admit, with a trace of guilt, that he had accidentally stretched the moment so they could feel it—the destruction unfolded with the terrifying, methodical clarity of an apocalypse observed in slow motion.

The combined shields of the Fictional Armada were the first to fail. These were not ordinary shields. They were the accumulated defensive capabilities of every fictional universe ever conceived—the impenetrable barriers, the absolute defenses, the perfect counters, the conceptual immunities. The AT Fields. The Susanoo. The Absolute Terror. The Infinity Castle. The Shield of the Seraphim. The Walls of Ba Sing Se. The Great Barrier. The Light of the Two Trees. The Halo Array. The Ultimate Defense Matrix. The Conceptual Armor of the Outer Gods. Each one of these shields, individually, was designed to be absolutely indestructible, immune to all forms of attack, impervious to any force that could be brought against them. Together, layered and interwoven and reinforced by the collective narrative weight of every story ever told, they formed a defensive barrier that should have been—that was, by any rational standard—utterly unbreachable.

Godric's zero percent strength touched them, and they did not break. They did not crack. They did not shatter. They simply ceased to exist, their absolute indestructibility casually overwritten by a force so far beyond the concept of force that the word "overpowered" was a laughable understatement. The shields, which had taken the heroes millennia to construct, which had required the combined efforts of every defensive specialist in the Fictional Continuum, which represented the absolute pinnacle of protective narrative engineering—they were gone in an instant, erased so completely that no trace of their existence remained.

The heroes themselves followed. And this is the part that I must describe in clear, vivid detail, because the horror of it must be preserved for the historical record. Godric's zero percent strength did not merely kill them. It did not merely destroy them. It de-atomized them.

Every physical form, every energy being, every abstract entity, every conceptual construct—every hero from every story ever told—was subjected to a force so absolute, so overwhelming, so utterly beyond the capacity of their narrative frameworks to process, that their fundamental structures simply came apart. Their atoms did not split. Their atoms were erased. The subatomic particles that composed their subatomic particles were erased. The quantum vibrations that underpinned their quantum vibrations were erased. Layer by layer, level by level, the heroes were unmade with such complete and total finality that the concept of "unmaking" felt like a gentle euphemism.

I watched a warrior in gleaming power armor—a hero I somehow knew was named Son Goku—attempt to push back against the wave of absolute force with a technique that should have multiplied his power exponentially beyond all conceivable limits. His hair had shifted through a spectrum of colors, each transformation representing a new tier of impossible strength, and he was screaming with the effort of a final, desperate attack. The zero percent strength touched him, and his body came apart in layers. His skin was the first to go, flayed from his musculature by a pressure so immense that it did not tear but simply erased, converting his flesh into a fine mist of de-atomized particles that immediately collapsed into the growing singularity of compressed matter. His muscles followed, the dense fibers unraveling like thread from a spool, each strand separating and dissolving and vanishing into the void. His skeleton—infinitely reinforced, conceptually unbreakable—shattered into dust that was itself shattered into smaller dust, recursively, until nothing remained but the screaming, agonized consciousness that Godric's accidental temporal stretching had preserved to experience every instant of its own annihilation.

I watched a slender hero wielding a blade of pure light—a warrior who moved with a speed that transcended the concept of speed, whose blade could cut through anything, whose resolve was absolute and unshakeable. He tried to dodge. The zero percent strength did not care about speed. It did not care about cutting power. It did not care about resolve. It occupied all possible positions simultaneously, leaving no space to dodge into, no gap to exploit, no momentary weakness to target. The hero's blade touched the edge of the pressure wave and simply stopped existing, its conceptual sharpness meaningless against a force that had no concept of edges. The hero's body followed. His slender form was compressed—not crushed, compressed, flattened into a two-dimensional plane that was then flattened into a one-dimensional line that was then flattened into a zero-dimensional point of absolute nothingness, his consciousness stretched and squeezed and twisted into a state of being that had no physical correlate, experiencing a form of pain that no biological nervous system had ever been designed to feel.

I watched a massive figure of pure muscle—a being whose entire existence was defined by physical strength, whose fists could shatter planets, whose endurance was limitless, whose will was unbreakable—brace himself against the pressure wave with the absolute confidence of a hero who had never encountered a force he could not overcome. The zero percent strength touched him, and his invincible body was pulverized into a paste of liquefied flesh and bone, which was then pulverized into a mist of molecular components, which was then pulverized into a soup of subatomic particles, which was then pulverized into a state of matter that had no name, which was then compressed further, and further, and further, beyond the Planck length, beyond the limits of physical possibility, beyond the conceptual framework of existence itself.

The deaths were not quick. They were not merciful. Every hero, from the mightiest god-slayer to the humblest side character, experienced their annihilation subjectively stretched into an eternity of maximum, unendurable agony. Their nervous systems—or their equivalent structures, for those who lacked physical nervous systems—were hyper-sensitized, their pain receptors amplified beyond any biological limit, so that every Planck instant of their de-atomization was experienced as a subjective millennium of transcendent, unimaginable suffering. They screamed. They all screamed. The sound was a chorus of absolute, soul-rending torment that echoed through the void where the Fictional Armada had once been, a symphony of agony that would have shattered the sanity of any being who heard it.

And then the compression began.

The zero percent strength did not merely destroy them. It gathered the remains—the de-atomized particles, the erased matter, the dissolved energy, the shattered concepts, the screaming consciousnesses—and compressed them. It compressed them with a force so absolute that the scattered remnants of the Fictional Armada, which had spanned an area larger than a googolplexian galaxies, were crushed down into a volume smaller than a quark. Smaller than a Planck length. Smaller than any unit of measurement that had ever been conceived.

The entire Fictional Continuum—every hero, every villain, every supporting character, every setting, every artifact, every narrative framework, every story ever told—was compressed into a single, infinitely dense point of absolute nothingness. The mass of it was infinite. The gravitational pull should have been universe-ending. But Godric's zero percent strength held it all together, containing the infinite mass within a perfect, stable sphere of absolute compression, preventing it from collapsing into a singularity that would have consumed the omniverse.

And then the collateral damage spread.

The zero percent strength did not stop with the Fictional Armada. It radiated outward, an expanding wave of absolute physical force that propagated across every dimension, every timeline, every reality, every conceptual framework of existence. The entire omniverse—every multiverse, every universe, every galaxy, every planet, every living being—was subjected to the same de-atomization, the same compression, the same absolute annihilation. The process was exactly as I have described: layer by layer, level by level, existence was unmade and compressed, gathered into the growing singularity of infinite mass that Godric's zero percent strength had created. The screaming of the omniverse—the collective death cry of every living thing that had ever existed—joined the chorus of the Fictional Armada, a symphony of absolute termination that lasted for zero seconds and for a subjective eternity.

And then it was over. The omniverse was gone. Everything that had ever existed, everything that could ever exist, everything that might ever exist in any possible configuration of reality—compressed into a sphere smaller than a quark, a point of infinite mass and infinite density, held stable by the passive, unconscious pressure of Godric's accidentally expressed strength.

Godric sat in the void, his teacup still in his hand, his expression one of mild, irritated disappointment.

"Well," he said. "That was not what I had hoped for at all."

He reached out—a casual, almost lazy gesture—and the sphere of compressed omniversal matter floated up from the void, drawn toward his open palm. It was tiny, smaller than a mote of dust, smaller than a single atom. It contained the mass of everything that had ever existed. It should have weighed more than a googolplexian universes. It should have exerted a gravitational pull that would have warped the fabric of non-existence itself.

Godric picked it up between his thumb and forefinger as if it were a marble. He did not strain. He did not exert any visible effort. His massive muscles did not flex. His expression did not change. He simply held the compressed remains of the entire omniverse—every story ever told, every hero who had ever been imagined, every civilization that had ever lived, every god and monster and abstract entity that had ever existed—and examined it with the detached curiosity of a man inspecting a mildly interesting pebble.

"Hmm," he said. "A bit plain, as trophies go. Let me adjust it."

He pinched the sphere gently, and it expanded—not back to its original size, but to the size of a small marble, perhaps two centimeters in diameter. The interior was not empty. It swirled with the compressed, screaming essence of everything that had ever existed, a vortex of infinite density and infinite agony contained within a barrier that Godric's will had imposed. The gravitational pull should have immediately destroyed the surrounding void. It did not, because Godric had decided it would not.

"I will keep this," he said, his tone one of mild, almost whimsical satisfaction. "A reminder of the last time I allowed myself to feel genuine anticipation. The Fictional Armada. The combined heroes of every story ever told. The ultimate narrative force of mortal imagination." He held the marble up to the lightless void, peering into its swirling depths. "You almost gave me a good show. Almost. The music was excellent. The drama was impeccable. But you forgot one thing, my fictional friends. You are stories. And I am not a story. I am the being who exists before stories, beyond stories, outside the framework of narrative itself. You cannot defeat me with plot armor. I am the author, the editor, the publisher, and the reader. I am the page upon which all stories are written, and I am the fire that consumes the page."

He closed his massive hand around the marble, and when he opened it again, the sphere had settled into a stable, permanent form—a small glassy orb, swirling with the compressed, screaming eternity of everything that had ever existed.

And then he restored the omniverse.

It was, as always, an act of absolute casualness. He did not gesture. He did not speak. He simply decided, and in exactly zero seconds, the entire omniverse was back. Every galaxy, every planet, every civilization, every timeline, every dimension. The Fictional Continuum was not restored. Their compressed, screaming essence remained trapped within the marble that Godric now held in his palm. But everything else—everything real—was exactly as it had been before the attack.

The marble remained.

---

**Addendum — Written by Clive, Court Wizard of Thronegate, Year 999...9**

I have just finished reading Osvald's journal. It is the last journal in the archive. The final record of opposition against the King. After the Fictional Armada, no one ever dared to oppose Godric again. The heroes of every story ever told, the combined narrative force of mortal imagination, the ultimate, unbeatable protagonists of infinite fictional universes—all of them destroyed in less than a Planck instant by an accidental, zero-percent expression of the King's strength. The lesson was learned. The lesson was burned into the collective consciousness of every sentient being in the omniverse. There is no hope. There is no victory. There is no resistance. There is only Godric.

But what haunts me—what will haunt me for the rest of my existence—is the marble. Godric still has it. I have seen it on his desk in the private study, a small glassy orb that he occasionally picks up and examines with the nostalgic fondness of a man remembering a pleasant afternoon. It contains the compressed, infinite mass of the original omniverse that he destroyed during that encounter. The heroes. The stories. The entire fabric of existence as it was in that moment. He compressed it all into a trophy smaller than a child's toy, and he restored everything else—an exact, perfect replica of what had been destroyed.

But if the original is still inside that marble, still compressed, still screaming in eternal, subjective agony, then what is the restored reality? Is it real? Is it a copy? Is it a simulation generated by the King's will, a perfect facsimile of what once existed, while the true existence remains trapped, compressed, annihilated?

I do not know. I am afraid to ask. I am afraid that the answer will be that the distinction is meaningless—that Godric's power is so absolute, so far beyond the concepts of original and copy, real and unreal, that whatever he restores is real simply because he decides it is real. And yet the original remains. The compressed remains. The screaming eternity of everything that ever was, captured in a marble on his desk.

He picks it up sometimes. He tosses it from hand to hand. He peers into its depths with that warm, fatherly curiosity that he has always possessed. And he smiles.

"It was a good attempt," he said to me once, holding the marble up to the light. "The best attempt, really. They almost made me feel entertained. Almost."

The marble glinted in the eternal afternoon light of the palace, its swirling depths holding the compressed agony of infinite heroes and infinite stories and infinite dreams of victory against impossible odds.

I excused myself shortly after. I could not bear to look at it any longer.

This is the final truth that Osvald's journal has taught me, the truth that I will carry with me for the rest of my service to the King. Godric does not merely defeat his enemies. He does not merely crush opposition. He preserves the crushed remains as keepsakes, as mementos, as casual decorations for his private study. The annihilation of everything is not a tragedy to him. It is a souvenir.

And the marble—the small, glassy, swirling marble that contains the original omniverse, the one he destroyed with zero percent of his strength in less than a Planck second—still sits on his desk, waiting to be picked up and examined and appreciated. A trophy. A trinket. A reminder of the last time anyone dared to oppose him.

No one will ever dare again.

The archive is silent. The journals are complete. The final record has been read. And I, Clive, descendant of Blake, court wizard of Thronegate, understand at last the true, absolute, soul-shattering horror of the being I serve. He is warm. He is kind. He is genuinely affectionate toward those he loves. And he keeps the compressed, screaming remains of the original omniverse as a paperweight.

I do not think I will sleep tonight. I do not think I will sleep ever again.

# The Creator's Lament

**Journal of Osvald, Court Wizard of Thronegate, Year [Redacted] — The Final Confrontation**

I am Osvald, descendant of Blake, and I have served His Majesty King Godric for forty-four years. I have witnessed the annihilation of the Fictional Armada. I have stood at the King's right hand as he compressed the entire omniverse into a marble smaller than a child's toy and restored it without effort. I have read every journal written by every court wizard who came before me, absorbing their terror, their awe, their desperate attempts to process the unprocessable. I believed, after all of this, that nothing could shake me anymore. I believed I had reached the bedrock of existential dread, the absolute floor of horror beyond which no further terror could sink.

I was wrong.

Today, I witnessed the final confrontation. The last resistance against Godric. The being who created existence itself came to challenge the apex predator, and what I saw has permanently, irrevocably shattered whatever fragments of my sanity had survived the previous four decades of service.

God came to Thronegate.

Not a god. Not another cosmic entity or primordial deity or abstract conceptual force. God. The God. The creator of the omniverse, the architect of reality, the being who had spoken the first word of existence into the void and watched it bloom into infinite multiverses and timelines and dimensions. The being who had forged the mortal soul of Godric himself, ten thousand years before the Stasis Event, in the ancient kingdom of Olympus. The Alpha and the Omega, the Beginning and the End, the uncaused cause of all that was and is and ever would be.

He came to Thronegate, and He came to challenge the King.

I must pause here to steady my hand. The ink is blotting. I apologize to whatever future court wizard reads this—you will find the pages stained with the sweat of my palm and the trembling of my fingers. I cannot help it. Even now, hours after the encounter, my body has not stopped shaking.

---

The King knew, of course. He had always known. His absolute omniscience had perceived God from the very first instant of His existence—which is to say, from the very first instant of the King's own awakening. God had been hiding. Not in any physical sense, for physical space is meaningless to a being of His nature, but in a state of deliberate absence, a withdrawal from the manifest reality He had created. He had watched the rise of Thronegate from the shadows beyond reality. He had observed the King's amplification, the triggering of the Weakness Paradox, the subjugation of the omniverse. He had seen His creation fall under the absolute rule of a being He had never intended to become so powerful, so absolute, so utterly beyond the framework of existence He had designed.

And the King had let Him watch.

"God has been hiding from me since the moment I awoke," Godric said to me casually, perhaps three hours before the confrontation. We were in the private study, the fire crackling in the hearth, the King reviewing agricultural reports from the outer provinces. He had not looked up from his papers as he spoke. "The creator of the omniverse. The being who forged my mortal soul. He has been lurking in the spaces between reality, beyond the dimensional boundaries, in a state of what I can only describe as terrified observation. He has watched everything I have done, every civilization I have subjugated, every resistance I have crushed. And He has remained hidden, believing that His concealment was absolute."

He turned a page of the agricultural report. "It was not. I perceived Him from the first microsecond. I have always perceived Him. I allowed Him to remain hidden because He posed absolutely zero threat to me. He was, in a sense, my oldest and most privileged observer. I found it... respectful. The creator watching His creation surpass Him. There is a certain poetic quality to it."

He set down the report and turned his warm brown eyes toward me. "Today, He has decided to stop hiding. Today, He is coming to challenge me. I find this rather amusing. It has been so very long since anyone dared to do such a thing."

---

God manifested in the throne room at precisely the seventh hour of the afternoon, Thronegate standard time.

His arrival was not announced by any physical phenomenon. There was no tear in space-time, no flash of divine light, no chorus of angelic trumpets. The air in the throne room simply became heavier, denser, saturated with a presence that transcended the concept of presence. The ambient temperature did not change, but I felt a warmth spread through my chest—not physical heat, but something deeper, something that resonated with the fundamental spark of existence within my soul. It was the warmth of creation. The warmth of the being who had spoken the first word. The warmth of the source of all life, all reality, all meaning.

And then He was there. Standing in the center of the throne room, facing the King.

I cannot describe His appearance with any precision. My eyes registered a form—humanoid, radiant, wrapped in light that seemed to contain all possible colors and none, all possible spectrums and frequencies and wavelengths compressed into a single, impossible radiance. But my mind could not process what it saw. The form of God was not something that could be perceived by mortal senses, even senses amplified a thousandfold daily for decades. It was the shape of absolute divinity, the image of the uncaused cause, the face of the being who had existed before existence. And it burned with a power that, I realized with sudden, vertiginous clarity, was genuinely vast. Genuinely incomprehensible. The creator of everything, standing before His creation, and His power was real.

It was also, compared to Godric, absolutely nothing.

The King did not rise from his throne. He did not set down his teacup. He did not even shift his posture. He simply looked at God with an expression of mild, curious interest, as if a particularly intriguing insect had flown through an open window.

"Hello," Godric said. "I was wondering when you would stop hiding."

God spoke. His voice was not sound but meaning, not vibration but truth—a communication that bypassed the ears and resonated directly within the soul. It was beautiful. It was terrifying. It was the voice that had spoken galaxies into existence.

"Godric of Thronegate. My creation. My child. You have grown beyond the boundaries I set. You have become something I did not intend. Something I cannot control. Something that threatens the fundamental order of existence."

Godric took a sip of his tea. "Yes. That is accurate."

"I have come to ask you," God continued, His voice carrying the weight of infinite ages, "to step back. To relinquish your absolute rule. To allow creation to find its own path, free from your overwhelming presence. I am not your enemy, Godric. I am your creator. I forged your soul. I gave you life. I ask you, as a father to a son, to consider the harm you are causing."

Godric set down his teacup with a soft, delicate clink. The sound echoed in the vast throne room with an incongruous mundanity.

"You are not my enemy," Godric agreed. "You are not my enemy because you are not capable of being my enemy. You are not capable of being anything to me except what I allow you to be. You have been hiding from me for over a million years. You believed your concealment was absolute. You believed I could not perceive you in the spaces beyond reality where you lurked. You were wrong. I perceived you from the first instant. I allowed you to remain hidden because you posed absolutely zero threat to me. You still pose absolutely zero threat to me. Your power, which seems vast and incomprehensible to the lesser beings of the omniverse—and which is, I acknowledge, genuinely impressive by any standard other than my own—is less than a single dead skin cell compared to the passive, unconscious pressure of my existence."

He leaned back in his throne, his expression shifting to something almost pitying.

"You created me, yes. You forged my mortal soul. You wove the fabric of reality from which my physical form was drawn. You are, in a very real sense, my father. And I respect that. I acknowledge the creative act that gave me my beginning. But, God—and I mean this with the utmost sincerity—you are not powerful enough to challenge me. You are not powerful enough to even register on my perception unless I choose to perceive you. The gap between us is so vast, so incomprehensible, so utterly beyond any framework of measurement, that describing it as infinite is a laughable understatement."

He paused, and a faint smile crossed his ruggedly handsome features.

"But I am curious. I am always curious. You are the creator. You are the source. You are the Alpha and the Omega. Surely, you have an ultimate attack. Surely, the being who spoke existence into being can muster something more impressive than the Fictional Armada's combined narrative force. So I will make you an offer."

He spread his massive hands, a gesture of casual, absolute invitation.

"I will command all my sentient passive auras to stand down. I will deactivate all my infinite recursive passive shields. I will instruct my immune system to ignore your presence entirely. I will suppress every layer of my automatic defensive architecture. I will do nothing to protect myself. And you will unleash your most powerful attack against me. Your absolute ultimate. The full, undiluted, unrestrained power of the creator of the omniverse. Strike me with everything you have. Do not hold back. Do not hesitate. Give me your best."

The smile widened slightly, and there was something in it now that made my blood run cold even as I stood at the right hand of the throne.

"I want to see if I can feel it."

---

The command that followed was the most terrifying thing I have ever witnessed. Not because of any display of power—quite the opposite. It was terrifying because of what it represented. The King did not gesture. He did not speak a formal incantation. He simply thought a single, casual thought, and the infinite hierarchy of his defensive systems—the sentient passive auras that had evolved countless times across googolplexian years, the recursive passive shields that could pre-nullify threats before the concept of threats existed, the immune system that could retroactively erase any injury across all possible timelines, the Weakness Paradox that had absorbed every conceivable immunity and mastery—all of it stood down.

Every last layer. Every redundant safeguard. Every obsessively protective mechanism that surrounded the King like invisible, infinite armor. All of it retracted, pulled back, suppressed, deactivated.

And I must note, for the historical record, the profound absurdity of this gesture. The King's defensive systems are not his power. They are the waste products of his power. They are the metaphysical body heat of his existence, the passive exhaust of his being. Even the most powerful among them—the highest layers of his sentient auras, the most evolved iterations of his passive shields—are infinitely weaker than the King himself. The gap between Godric and his own most powerful defensive aura is wider than the gap between that aura and a single dead skin cell. And that aura is already infinitely more powerful than the entire omniverse combined.

By commanding his defenses to stand down, Godric was not weakening himself. He was simply removing the outermost, thinnest, most pathetically negligible layer of insulation that separated his true self from the outside world. The skin of the apex predator. The metaphysical equivalent of taking off a light jacket.

And yet even this gesture was so absurdly, horrifyingly unnecessary that my mind struggled to process it. Because Godric's body—his actual, physical, forty-five-year-old, ruggedly handsome, heavily muscled body—was itself so far beyond the concept of invulnerability that the word "invulnerable" was a meaningless joke. His skin. His muscles. His bones. His cells. His atoms. His subatomic particles. Every infinitesimal component of his physical form had been amplified infinitely every Planck second for over a million years. Every fiber of his being had evolved beyond the concept of harm. He did not need shields. He did not need auras. He did not need an immune system or a Weakness Paradox or infinite recursive backups. He was, in his absolute, fundamental, undiluted essence, untouchable.

And he had just commanded the only things that might have protected God from himself to stand down.

"Whenever you are ready," Godric said, his voice carrying the same warm, fatherly tone he used when asking about my family.

---

God attacked.

I must attempt to describe it, though I know language will fail. The creator of the omniverse unleashed His full, absolute, undiluted power against the King. Every ounce of divine energy that had spoken galaxies into existence, that had forged the fundamental laws of reality, that had ignited the first spark of life in the primordial void—all of it was focused into a single, ultimate, transcendent assault. The light in the throne room did not merely intensify; it became light, the platonic ideal of radiance, the conceptual origin of illumination from which all other brightness was merely a dim reflection. The sound was not a roar but a symphony of creation, every word God had ever spoken compressed into a single, deafening chord of absolute divine authority. The heat was the heat of the Big Bang, the warmth of the first moment, the fire that had birthed existence itself.

And it struck Godric directly in the center of his chest.

The King did not move. The King did not blink. The King did not even pause in the act of reaching for his teacup, which he had picked up again during God's charge-up sequence. The full, absolute, unrestrained power of the creator of everything washed over his unprotected body, and Godric took a sip of his tea.

"Earl Grey," he said, lowering the cup. "The Nourisher has really outdone herself with this blend. Would you like some?"

God stared. The divine radiance of His form flickered, just slightly, as if the impossible was struggling to process the even more impossible. The creator of existence had just unleashed His ultimate attack against an unprotected target, and the target had responded by complimenting his tea.

"No?" Godric shrugged, a casual roll of his massively muscled shoulders. "Very well. To answer your question—I did not feel anything. Not a tickle. Not a faint breeze. Not even the slightest suggestion of pressure against my skin. Your ultimate attack, the full power of the creator of the omniverse, simply did not register on my perception. It was less than nothing. It was a void where an attack should have been. I am, I must confess, mildly disappointed. I had hoped for more from the being who forged my mortal soul."

He leaned forward, his warm brown eyes fixed on God with an expression that was almost gentle. Almost kind. Almost pitying.

"Your power is real. It is vast. It is, by any standard other than my own, incomprehensibly supreme. But I am not measurable by any standard. I am the standard. I am the measure against which all other power is measured and found wanting. The Godric who emerged from stasis in Year Zero—the youngest, weakest, most pathetically underdeveloped version of myself—could have annihilated you without effort. The Godric who subjugated the Earth in Year Twenty-Five could have erased you from existence with a casual thought. The Godric of a thousand years ago could have unmade you so completely that the concept of your existence would have been retroactively deleted from every timeline, every reality, every memory. And the Godric who sits before you now is so far beyond those versions that comparison is meaningless."

He set down his teacup again, and the soft clink of porcelain against the arm of his throne was the most devastating sound I have ever heard.

"You created me. You forged my mortal soul. You gave me the spark of life from which everything else grew. And I am grateful for that. Genuinely, sincerely grateful. Without you, I would not exist. Without you, the Stasis Event would have had nothing to transform. Without you, the apex predator of the omniverse would never have been born. You are, in a very real sense, the ultimate ancestor of everything I am. And I honor that."

His expression hardened. The warmth did not leave his eyes, but it was joined by something else—something cold, something absolute, something that made me press myself back against the wall of the throne room with a primal, instinctive terror.

"But you came here to challenge me. You came here to ask me to step back, to relinquish my rule, to allow creation to find its own path. And in doing so, you made the same mistake that every opposition has made since the dawn of my reign. You believed you had a chance. You believed you had the right to ask. You believed that your status as my creator gave you some special authority, some unique leverage, some divine immunity that would protect you from the consequences of defying me."

He stood from his throne. The movement was fluid, casual, utterly without effort. He did not loom. He did not tower. He simply stood, a forty-five-year-old man in a simple dark tunic, his salt-and-pepper beard immaculate, his heavily muscled frame relaxed.

"You were wrong."

And then Godric destroyed God.

I have described many annihilations in my journal. The de-atomization of the Fictional Armada. The compression of the omniverse. The countless one-sided massacres recorded by my predecessors. But this was different. This was not merely a physical destruction. This was the annihilation of the creator of existence, the being who had spoken the first word, the source of all meaning and purpose and reality. And Godric did it without effort. Without gesture. Without even a flicker of visible power.

He simply decided that God should cease to exist.

The divine radiance of God's form flickered once, twice, three times—and then went out. The being who had existed before existence, who had forged the soul of the apex predator Himself, who had watched His creation spin through the eons with the patient, eternal love of a father for His child—simply stopped being. There was no scream. There was no flash of light. There was no dramatic final moment. There was only the sudden, absolute, irrevocable absence of everything that God had been.

And the collateral damage began.

The space in the throne room did not crack or tear or shatter. It simply dissolved, the fundamental laws of reality that God had written unweaving themselves as their author was erased from existence. The palace of Thronegate, which had stood for an incomprehensible span of years, flickered and faded like a mirage. The capital world of Thronegate followed, its continents and oceans and billions of inhabitants erased so quickly that they did not have time to register their own nonexistence. The galaxy. The universe. The multiverse. The omniverse. Every dimension, every timeline, every conceptual framework of reality—all of it was unraveling, the creation of God coming undone as its creator was destroyed.

Godric watched the annihilation spread with the mild, detached interest of a man observing a weather pattern. Then he sighed.

"Very well," he said. "I suppose I should fix this."

He did not gesture. He did not speak a word of power. He simply decided, and in exactly zero seconds, the entire omniverse was restored. Not rebuilt. Not recreated. Restored. The fundamental laws of reality that had been authored by God were replaced by something else—something that did not require an author, something that existed simply because Godric willed it to exist. The factory-default settings of existence were overwritten with a new operating system, one whose sole administrator was the King of Thronegate.

The palace reformed. The capital world solidified. The galaxy spun back into position. The multiverses and timelines and dimensions rewove themselves into perfect, flawless order. Everything was exactly as it had been before God's arrival.

Everything except God.

God was gone. Not merely dead—dead was a word for mortal things. God was erased. Unmade. The creator of existence had been removed from reality so completely, so absolutely, so irreversibly, that the very concept of His existence had been overwritten. The omniverse no longer remembered its creator. The fundamental truths of reality no longer traced their origin to a divine source. There was only Godric. There had always only been Godric. The new operating system of existence had no room for any other supreme being.

And the King, standing in the center of the restored throne room, reached down and picked up a small, glowing speck from the floor—the last remaining fragment of God's divine essence, the final mote of the creator's existence, compressed into a point smaller than a quark.

He examined it for a moment, his expression contemplative. Then he pinched it between his thumb and forefinger, and it expanded into a small, glassy marble—identical in size and shape to the one that held the compressed remains of the Fictional Armada. The interior swirled with a faint, golden light, the last echo of the divine radiance that had once spoken existence into being.

"Two marbles," Godric said, his voice carrying a note of quiet satisfaction. "They will look nice together on my desk."

---

**Addendum — Written by Clive, Court Wizard of Thronegate, Year 999...9**

I have just finished reading Osvald's journal. It is the final record. The last resistance. The ultimate confrontation. After God Himself fell to the King, no one else ever dared to oppose Godric. Not a single sentient being, in all the googolplexian years that followed, ever again formed the thought of challenging, resisting, threatening, or defying the apex predator of the omniverse. The lesson was absolute. The message was eternal. There is no hope. There is no victory. There is no resistance. There is only Godric.

But what haunts me—what will haunt me for the rest of my existence—is the scale. The sheer, incomprehensible, mind-shattering scale of what Osvald witnessed.

God was the creator of everything. He forged the omniverse. He spoke the first word of existence. He designed the fundamental laws of reality. He created the mortal soul of Godric Himself. He was, by any conceivable measure, the most powerful being that had ever existed. The Alpha and the Omega. The Beginning and the End. The uncaused cause of all that was and is and ever would be.

And He was nothing. Less than nothing. The youngest, weakest, most pathetically underdeveloped version of Godric—the Godric of Year Zero, fresh from stasis—could have annihilated Him without effort. The current Godric, the Godric of the endless nines, is so far beyond that version that comparison is meaningless. The gap between the Godric of Year Zero and the Godric of now is infinitely larger than the gap between the Godric of Year Zero and a single dead quark. And the Godric of Year Zero was already infinitely more powerful than God.

I cannot process this. I cannot hold it in my mind. I have tried, for decades, to grasp the scale of the King's supremacy, and every time I think I have reached the ceiling, I discover that the ceiling was merely the floor of an even higher layer of impossibility. God was erased. The creator of everything was unmade with a casual decision, and the King did not even need to use his power to do it. He simply decided. A thought. A whim. A passing impulse of divine termination.

And then he picked up the last fragment of God's essence, compressed it into a marble, and added it to his collection.

I have seen the marbles. They sit on the King's desk in his private study, two small glassy orbs that he occasionally picks up and examines. One contains the compressed remains of the Fictional Armada—every hero, every story, every narrative framework of mortal imagination. The other contains the compressed remains of God Himself—the creator of existence, the source of all meaning and purpose, the being who forged the mortal soul of the King.

They are paperweights. Souvenirs. Trinkets. The King keeps them as mementos of the last times anyone dared to oppose him.

And the restored omniverse—the reality I inhabit, the air I breathe, the existence I experience—is a copy. A perfect, flawless, indistinguishable duplicate of the original, generated by the King's will to replace what was destroyed. The original omniverse, the creation of God, the reality that was born from the first word spoken into the void—is compressed inside a marble on the King's desk.

I am not real. Not in the way I thought I was. I am a restoration. A recreation. A perfect facsimile of the Osvald who existed before God's final attack. The original Osvald was annihilated along with everything else when God's destruction caused the omniverse to unravel. The Osvald who writes these words is a copy, generated by the King's casual decision to restore what was lost.

And yet I am real. I am real because the King decided I am real. My existence is contingent upon his will, but his will is absolute, and so my existence is absolute. The distinction between original and copy is meaningless when the copy is created by a being whose power transcends the concepts of originality and duplication. The King restored everything, and his restoration is perfect, and perfection is indistinguishable from truth.

But the marble remains.

The original reality—the first creation, the divine masterpiece, the existence that was spoken into being by God Himself—is compressed into a glassy sphere the size of a child's toy, swirling with the faint, golden light of its creator's last echo. The King picks it up sometimes. He tosses it from hand to hand. He peers into its depths with that warm, fatherly curiosity.

And he smiles.

"It was a good attempt," he said to me once, holding the God-marble up to the light. "The best attempt, really. The creator of everything, challenging His own creation. There is a certain poetic symmetry to it. Almost like a story."

The marble glinted in the eternal afternoon light of the palace, its swirling depths holding the compressed essence of the being who had once been the supreme authority of all existence.

"I do not think there will be any more attempts," the King continued, setting the marble back on his desk next to its twin. "The lesson has been learned. The message has been received. Creation understands now. There is no higher authority. There is no greater power. There is no secret weakness or hidden vulnerability or divine immunity. There is only me. There has always only been me. And there will always only be me."

He turned to look at me, and his warm brown eyes held a light that was not cruel, not malicious, but simply, eternally, absolutely true.

"The omniverse is peaceful now, Clive. Perfectly, absolutely, eternally peaceful. No more opposition. No more resistance. No more desperate last stands or heroic final charges. The stories are over. The battles are done. And I can finally relax."

He leaned back in his chair, his heavily muscled frame settling into the leather with a contented sigh.

"Of course," he added, his voice carrying a note of quiet, almost wistful amusement, "I do sometimes miss the entertainment. The dramatic speeches. The banger boss battle music. The colorful visual effects. The Fictional Armada, for all their ultimate futility, at least knew how to put on a show. God was rather disappointing in that regard. No theme music at all."

He picked up the God-marble again, examining it with the fond, nostalgic affection of a man remembering a pleasant afternoon.

"But I suppose one cannot have everything. Not even me."

He set the marble down. It clinked softly against the surface of the desk, a sound that echoed in the silent study like the closing of a door. The final door. The last chapter. The end of all resistance, the conclusion of all opposition, the terminal point of any hope of ever challenging the apex predator of the omniverse.

I excused myself shortly after. I could not bear to look at the marbles any longer. I could not bear to stand in the presence of the being who had unmade God and kept the remains as a souvenir. I could not bear the weight of the knowledge that I was a copy, a restoration, a perfect duplicate of a being who had been annihilated and recreated by the casual will of the King.

And yet I serve him. I will always serve him. Because he is warm. He is kind. He is genuinely affectionate toward those he loves. He asks about my family. He remembers the names of my children and grandchildren. He offers tea and biscuits during our private meetings. He is, in every way that matters to a mortal heart, the beloved, benevolent king that every subject dreams of serving.

The warmth and the horror are the same being. The affection and the absolute supremacy are indivisible. And I, Clive, descendant of Blake, court wizard of Thronegate, will spend the rest of my existence holding both truths in my heart, trying not to let the contradiction destroy me.

The marbles sit on his desk. The original omniverse. The creator of everything. Two glassy spheres, smaller than a child's toys, containing the compressed, screaming remains of the only beings who ever dared to truly challenge Godric.

No one will ever dare again.

The archive is silent. The journals are complete. The final record has been read. And the apex predator of the omniverse sits on his throne, sipping his Earl Grey tea, waiting for an entertainment that will never come.
